item.title: Trump's Halloween flyover stunt terrifies Sept. 11 survivors
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used a low-altitude Air Force One flyover as part of a White House Halloween celebration, startling Washington residents—including people who lived through the September 11 attacks. Flight-tracking data cited by The Washington Post placed the aircraft between roughly 400 and 1,000 feet, while the White House promoted the spectacle as “epic.” The D.C. Council said downtown Washington, the Pentagon and Reagan National Airport received only
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used a low-altitude Air Force One flyover as part of a White House Halloween celebration, startling Washington residents—including people who lived through the September 11 attacks. Flight-tracking data cited by The Washington Post placed the aircraft between roughly 400 and 1,000 feet, while the White House promoted the spectacle as “epic.”

The D.C. Council said downtown Washington, the Pentagon and Reagan National Airport received only about 15 minutes’ notice. National Airport briefly stopped ground traffic, but several residents quoted by AlterNet said they did not know the aircraft was Air Force One until afterward; some thought a commercial plane might be crashing. Residents also reported shaking buildings and memories of Flight 77’s approach to the Pentagon.

The reporting does not establish that the administration intended to frighten anyone. It does establish that officials arranged a conspicuous flight through heavily restricted airspace, provided little public warning and celebrated the result without accounting for the predictable alarm.

Power made the spectacle

This was not an unauthorized pilot wandering into restricted airspace. Presidential control and federal aviation authority made the flyover possible. Government agencies managed the airspace, imposed a ground stop and accommodated a White House production.

That distinction matters because the startled residents had no comparable agency. They did not choose the route, altitude, timing or warning period. The administration possessed the information and institutional machinery needed to prevent panic. The people below possessed noise, a descending silhouette and 24 years of historical context.

Fifteen minutes is institutional failure

In Washington, a low-flying 747 is not politically neutral scenery. Restricted airspace exists partly because a passenger jet struck the Pentagon on September 11, 2001. The city also carried the recent memory, cited in the reporting, of the deadly 2025 collision near Reagan National Airport.

Under those conditions, 15 minutes’ notice was not meaningful public communication. An alert is useless to anyone who does not see it before the aircraft arrives. Residents quoted in the story said earlier notice—hours or a day, as with other flyovers—would likely have changed their reaction. The White House had access to that obvious precaution and apparently did not take it.

The sneer is part of the politics

Some online respondents called frightened residents stupid or mocked them for wanting advance warning. That response shifts responsibility downward: away from the officials who planned an unusual low-altitude flight and onto civilians who correctly recognized an aircraft where civilian aircraft ordinarily do not appear.

The mockery also invents a demand nobody made. Residents were not asking for personal clearance from the White House. They were asking the government to announce a government spectacle before staging it over a city shaped by an aerial terrorist attack. Treating that request as oversensitivity is not analysis. It is an excuse for administrative contempt.

Government as personal theater

The larger issue is the conversion of public authority into presidential stagecraft. Restricted airspace, aviation coordination and an iconic government aircraft became props for a Halloween video. The costs—disrupted airport operations, public alarm and revived trauma—were imposed on people who had no role in producing the performance.

That is a recognizable pattern of personalized power: institutions still perform their technical functions, but their purpose bends toward flattering the leader. The machinery works efficiently for the spectacle and poorly for those subjected to it. When preventable fear follows, supporters redirect scrutiny toward the frightened rather than the office that created the conditions.

The systemic error

The flyover was brief, but the governing habit it exposed is durable. Powerful officials make a discretionary choice; institutions enable it; inadequate communication transfers the risk to the public; and ridicule shields the decision-makers from accountability.

Calling the episode mere confusion would hide the chain of agency. The administration controlled the event and the warning. Residents controlled neither. A government that treats public space as a presidential set—and public alarm as somebody else’s embarrassment—is showing exactly whose experience counts once power decides it wants a show.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: 'Thank God': GOP secretly celebrates Trump's humiliating campaign retreat
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump canceled planned in-person campaign rallies in Salina, Kansas, on Oct. 31 and Iowa on Nov. 1, replacing them with tele-rallies shortly before the midterm elections. The article does not supply a year. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins cited unnamed Republican officials who welcomed the cancellations; one said, “Thank God,” because Trump had not improved the candidates’ position, while another said voters interested in seeing him already had. The Whi
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump canceled planned in-person campaign rallies in Salina, Kansas, on Oct. 31 and Iowa on Nov. 1, replacing them with tele-rallies shortly before the midterm elections. The article does not supply a year. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins cited unnamed Republican officials who welcomed the cancellations; one said, “Thank God,” because Trump had not improved the candidates’ position, while another said voters interested in seeing him already had.

The White House presented the shift as an opportunity for Trump to reach more people through more than 20 tele-rallies before Election Day. The Republican National Committee confirmed that the Kansas and Iowa events would not occur. AlterNet says Trump had already held more than two dozen rallies, but polling showed him underwater in Kansas, potentially making his presence a liability for Republican candidates.

Asked on Oct. 29 whether the Kansas cancellation reflected fatigue from traveling, Trump insulted the Reuters reporter’s health and appearance and said he simply did not need to visit Kansas. Collins characterized the question as straightforward and noted that Trump reacted as though his health had been challenged.

The power was never with the anonymous celebrants

The relieved Republican officials held enough proximity to power to complain privately, but apparently not enough independence—or courage—to speak publicly. Trump controlled the campaign spectacle. The White House controlled the official explanation. The RNC managed the event calendar. Candidates facing the electoral consequences were left to create distance without openly confronting the person dominating their party.

That hierarchy matters more than the private gloating. An unnamed official saying “Thank God” is not resistance. It is an admission that party professionals considered their own president politically damaging but depended on cancellation, rather than accountable leadership, to limit the damage.

A retreat sold as expanded reach

The White House did not describe the canceled rallies as a retreat. It reframed them as a more efficient national strategy: dozens of remote events, broader reach, direct contact with voters. That explanation may describe a genuine tactical advantage, but it does not answer why two announced appearances disappeared while Republican officials privately expressed relief.

The central political fact is the conflict between the public sales pitch and the party’s reported private assessment. Publicly, Trump remained an asset whose voice needed wider distribution. Privately, officials reportedly believed his physical presence no longer persuaded voters and could endanger candidates where his approval was weak.

The reporter became the decoy

Trump’s response redirected attention from a legitimate campaign question to the reporter’s body. Instead of explaining the cancellation, he called the journalist “sick,” “disgusting,” and “way out of shape.” The insult did political work: it replaced scrutiny of Trump’s usefulness, schedule, and decision-making with a manufactured confrontation.

The reporting should not let speculation about Trump’s health swallow the clearer issue. The Reuters question concerned whether travel fatigue influenced a canceled stop; the article does not establish that illness or exhaustion caused the change. What it does establish is that Trump declined to answer directly and attacked the person asking.

The party’s governing method is avoidance

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as campaign management. Republican officials reportedly recognized that Trump could hurt their candidates, yet their relief remained anonymous and their corrective action indirect. They wanted protection from his political liabilities without accepting responsibility for sustaining his authority.

That arrangement leaves voters with propaganda in public and candor only through leaks. The powerful actor is praised; weaker candidates quietly retreat; a reporter is abused for asking an ordinary question; and party officials celebrate backstage when circumstances spare them from confronting the leader they enabled. The systemic error is not merely Trump’s dominance. It is a party structure that treats honest acknowledgment of its own electoral judgment as more dangerous than the judgment itself.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump DOJ’s third Comey case faces a make-or-break courtroom test
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that James Comey’s lawyers were set to ask U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden in Washington, D.C., to dismiss the Justice Department’s third attempt to prosecute the former FBI director. The dispute centers on whether prosecutors could bypass a grand jury and file a “criminal information” to prevent the statute of limitations from expiring on an alleged 2016 media leak. The Justice Department said the filing preserved its ability to seek an indictment. Comey, who
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that James Comey’s lawyers were set to ask U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden in Washington, D.C., to dismiss the Justice Department’s third attempt to prosecute the former FBI director. The dispute centers on whether prosecutors could bypass a grand jury and file a “criminal information” to prevent the statute of limitations from expiring on an alleged 2016 media leak.

The Justice Department said the filing preserved its ability to seek an indictment. Comey, who maintains his innocence, argued that the maneuver was legally invalid. The allegation concerns anonymous disclosures about a secret surveillance order requiring Yahoo to scan emails for possible links to a foreign terrorist group.

Federal authorities had examined the episode twice before without filing charges. According to Comey’s court filing, John Durham recommended against prosecution in a classified December 2018 memorandum; a later investigation by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia closed without charges in February 2020.

The power is at Justice

Comey is not the institution exercising coercive power here. The Justice Department is. It decides whether to revive a decade-old allegation, seek criminal process and force a defendant to spend time and money resisting the state.

That distinction matters because the personal feud between Comey and Donald Trump can make the story look like a clash between two powerful antagonists. It is not an equal contest. Comey can publish criticism and file motions. The administration controls the department bringing the case.

McFadden, a Trump appointee, holds the immediate judicial authority to decide whether this procedural gambit survives. His appointment is relevant context, but it does not establish how he will rule.

A deadline is not an explanation

The department’s stated reason for filing without a grand-jury indictment is that the 10-year limitations period was approaching. That explains the timing of the maneuver, not why prosecutors decided the underlying matter deserved revival after earlier inquiries ended without charges.

The institutional question is therefore larger than whether a “criminal information” can stop the clock. Prosecutors revisited conduct already examined by Durham and by the D.C. U.S. Attorney’s Office. If the government now possesses materially different evidence, AlterNet’s account does not identify it. If it does not, the procedural urgency was created by the government’s own decision to reopen an old file.

Treating that urgency as an impersonal scheduling problem would conceal agency. Officials chose to proceed.

The feud obscures the machinery

Comey investigated possible coordination between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia, later compared Trump to a mafia boss, and became a recurring target of Trump’s public accusations and demands for imprisonment. That history supplies an obvious political context, but personal hostility is not the most consequential feature of the story.

The consequential feature is the conversion of hostility into repeated prosecutorial action. One case alleging that Comey lied to Congress was thrown out because the prosecutor had been appointed unlawfully. Another pending indictment alleges that an Instagram image reading “86 47” constituted a threat; Comey has sought dismissal. The latest matter revives the alleged leak.

Calling this merely a bitter relationship would misdirect attention from the actor with charging authority. Only one side of the feud commands federal prosecutors.

Prosecution can be the punishment

Comey remains presumed innocent, and the reporting does not establish that Justice Department officials fabricated evidence or brought charges solely to satisfy Trump. It does establish a pattern of repeated attempts: an invalidated prosecution, another disputed indictment and now a procedural effort to preserve a third case involving conduct from 2016.

Even unsuccessful prosecutions impose consequences. They consume resources, attach criminal allegations to political enemies and signal that previously closed matters can be reopened when control of the department changes. A dismissal may prevent a conviction while leaving that disciplinary effect intact.

The timing reported by AlterNet—amid several politically charged department actions before the midterms—raises the stakes. It does not prove electoral intent, but it makes scrutiny of the department’s evidence, procedures and departure from earlier decisions indispensable.

The systemic error

The narrow courtroom question is whether this filing method was lawful. The broader political question is whether prosecutorial discretion has become a renewable instrument against a president’s critics.

Institutions are not depoliticized simply because officials describe their choices in procedural language. Statutes of limitation, appointment rules and grand juries are constraints on state power, not inconveniences to be engineered around whenever an administration wants another attempt.

When coverage centers the animosity between Trump and Comey, it risks shrinking an institutional abuse question into personality drama. The durable danger lies in the precedent: executive power repeatedly testing legal boundaries until one prosecution finally sticks.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: 'Everybody's funeral': Trump biographer smells panic in the White House
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Michael Wolff told his podcast that a Republican defeat in the approaching midterm elections could trigger panic inside President Donald Trump’s White House. As reported by AlterNet via the Daily Beast, Wolff predicted that aides would face congressional investigations, legal bills, career damage, and blame from Trump—making the aftermath “everybody’s funeral.” Wolff said Democrats gaining congressional power would probably pursue officials around Trump rather than prioritize anoth
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Michael Wolff told his podcast that a Republican defeat in the approaching midterm elections could trigger panic inside President Donald Trump’s White House. As reported by AlterNet via the Daily Beast, Wolff predicted that aides would face congressional investigations, legal bills, career damage, and blame from Trump—making the aftermath “everybody’s funeral.”

Wolff said Democrats gaining congressional power would probably pursue officials around Trump rather than prioritize another impeachment that Senate Republicans could block. He identified Attorney General Todd Blanche as a likely target and alleged that Blanche had enabled legally futile actions against people Trump resented. Co-host Joanna Coles also pointed to announced Democratic plans involving Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

These were predictions made before the reported election, not evidence that subpoenas had been issued, investigations completed, or crimes established. AlterNet offered no independent reporting showing that White House officials were actually searching for lawyers; its central evidence was Wolff’s commentary.

Power before panic

The story’s imagery reverses the real hierarchy. Trump’s aides are not merely anxious employees trapped in someone else’s storm. They occupy the executive branch, direct federal departments, and can use public authority against designated targets. Their possible exposure matters precisely because they currently hold extraordinary institutional power.

Trump sits at the top of that structure. Congress, however, controls its own formidable machinery: committees, hearings, subpoenas, and impeachment proceedings. The election matters because it could transfer investigative power—not because accountability suddenly materializes from partisan emotion.

Agency does not disappear downward

Wolff portrays Trump as the expected source of blame and Blanche as an enabler who acts because Trump instructs him. That distinction identifies command, but it does not erase subordinate agency. An appointed official who carries out a president’s demands still makes decisions, exercises discretion, and attaches government power to those choices.

The article’s “henchmen” language gestures toward responsibility while its panic narrative risks recasting powerful officials as impending victims. Losing insulation from scrutiny is not the same as being powerless. Fear of subpoenas is a foreseeable consequence of governing in ways that attract legitimate questions.

Prediction is not proof

The weakest part of the framing is its reliance on Wolff’s certainty. He alleges corruption, anticipates legal jeopardy, and predicts Democratic retaliation, but the article supplies no underlying records, court findings, or identified conduct sufficient to establish criminal wrongdoing. “Smells panic” is a mood presented as news.

That does not make congressional scrutiny improper. It means the case for scrutiny must rest on documented official acts, not a biographer’s metaphor or an opponent’s appetite. Otherwise, the coverage mimics the politics it claims to diagnose: personalities replace evidence, and anticipated spectacle replaces institutional analysis.

Accountability or partisan theater

Calling prospective investigations “the wrath of the Democrats” misdirects attention from the actual standard. The central question is not whether Democrats are angry. It is whether executive officials misused public authority and whether Congress can establish that through evidence, testimony, and lawful process.

That framing also gives Trump’s circle a ready-made defense. Officials can describe oversight as vengeance while avoiding the substance of what they authorized. Democrats would reinforce that defense if they began with promised targets and impeachment rhetoric instead of specific conduct and a disciplined evidentiary record.

The system protects the apex

The larger pattern is familiar: concentrated presidential power flows downward, while accountability struggles to travel upward. Wolff expects Trump to blame aides, Senate Republicans to shield him from removal, and congressional investigators to pursue more vulnerable subordinates. Each institution follows its incentives, leaving the central holder of power comparatively insulated.

That is the systemic error. Government officials can spend years exercising authority through a leader-centered chain of command, then become expendable when political control shifts. Coverage turns the resulting scramble into palace drama. The more consequential story is how institutions permit power to be personalized at the top and responsibility to be scattered beneath it.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Choke with a charger: Trump official accused of bizarre threat
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Justice Department official Leo Terrell was accused of threatening to choke intern Tejas Billa with a computer charger after berating him for nearly an hour about leaving it at home. Billa and another intern reportedly described the September 16 exchange, including alleged threats to fire Billa. Terrell denied threatening either dismissal or violence. According to the account discussed by The Bulwark’s Sam Stein and Will Sommer, Billa reported the incident to
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Justice Department official Leo Terrell was accused of threatening to choke intern Tejas Billa with a computer charger after berating him for nearly an hour about leaving it at home. Billa and another intern reportedly described the September 16 exchange, including alleged threats to fire Billa. Terrell denied threatening either dismissal or violence.

According to the account discussed by The Bulwark’s Sam Stein and Will Sommer, Billa reported the incident to an official in the associate attorney general’s office and resigned nine days later. AlterNet also cites separate 2025 reporting that Terrell led the Justice Department’s antisemitism task force, promoted Trump administration policies, and reposted accounts described as having histories of antisemitic content.

Power was not ambiguous

Terrell was a Justice Department lawyer heading a federal task force. Billa was an intern. One possessed institutional authority, political access, and a social-media audience measured in millions; the other occupied one of the most disposable positions in government.

That imbalance is the political fact around which everything else turns. Even without resolving the disputed allegation, a subordinate reported threatening conduct and then left the department nine days later. The institution retained the senior official. AlterNet provides no indication that the complaint produced an investigation, discipline, or protection for the intern.

The institution had notice

The reported response from the official managing the associate attorney general’s office — “He’s been terrible, hasn’t he?” — matters because it suggests recognition rather than surprise. It does not independently prove a pattern, despite Sommer’s conclusion. It does indicate that Billa’s complaint was allegedly met with familiarity.

That is how institutional cowardice often presents itself: misconduct becomes office knowledge without becoming an institutional problem. Staff members learn whom to avoid, subordinates absorb the cost, and managers translate an abuse allegation into weary gossip. Authority remains undisturbed because the person reporting the conduct has less leverage than the person accused.

The spectacle obscures the failure

AlterNet frames the episode through two pundits marveling at its strangeness. The charger makes the allegation memorable, but “bizarre” is a weak political category. The serious question is not why Terrell was supposedly so angry about a missing cable. It is what the Justice Department did after an intern reported that a senior official had threatened his job and physical safety.

The article never establishes that answer. Its reliance on conversational reactions also muddies the evidence: Sommer’s claim that the exchange showed a pattern goes beyond what the quoted office response alone can prove. Sharp criticism requires sharper sourcing, especially when the accused has denied the central allegations.

Enforcement as political branding

Terrell’s position adds a grim contradiction. AlterNet cites reporting that the official leading a federal antisemitism task force publicly advocated punitive action against a Columbia graduate and the university while reposting accounts reported to have promoted antisemitism. That does not establish Terrell’s intent, but it raises a legitimate question about whether the task force’s stated mission matched the conduct surrounding its leader.

When enforcement offices become vehicles for partisan media performance, scrutiny flows outward while accountability disappears inward. The official promotes punishment for designated targets; the institution appears unable, at least in this account, to explain how it handled a complaint against him.

The system protects upward

The broader pattern is not merely an official accused of an ugly outburst. It is a hierarchy in which power determines whose conduct becomes policy and whose injury becomes attrition.

Billa reportedly complained and departed. Terrell denied the allegations and remained in command. Unless the Justice Department’s response changes that record, the consequence is plain: the weaker actor paid the visible price, while the institution’s exercise of power continued uninterrupted.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump accused of planning 'devastating' Iran escalation
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Sen. Chris Murphy said he had been briefed on a post-midterm plan by President Donald Trump’s administration to escalate military operations against Iran. Murphy withheld operational details but called the plan “insane,” predicted “devastating escalation,” and said it would likely undermine the rule of law without achieving its objectives. The report cites CNN’s earlier account that sufficient U.S. forces were already positioned in the region for attacks exten
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Sen. Chris Murphy said he had been briefed on a post-midterm plan by President Donald Trump’s administration to escalate military operations against Iran. Murphy withheld operational details but called the plan “insane,” predicted “devastating escalation,” and said it would likely undermine the rule of law without achieving its objectives.

The report cites CNN’s earlier account that sufficient U.S. forces were already positioned in the region for attacks extending beyond limited strikes on replaceable Iranian military assets. It also quotes political scientist John Mearsheimer arguing that the United States lacked leverage, faced munitions constraints, and risked Iranian retaliation against Gulf oil and desalination infrastructure. The article supplies no administration response, documentary war plan, or independent account of Murphy’s briefing, so the plan’s precise scope and legal basis remain unestablished.

The power is in the White House

Murphy’s warning is politically important, but he is not the actor directing the military. The institutional power belongs to Trump and the executive branch officials preparing, recommending, authorizing, and executing military operations.

That distinction matters because political coverage routinely turns an impending use of state violence into a dispute among commentators. A senator calls a plan reckless; a political scientist calls the existing campaign a defeat; strategists calculate electoral damage. But the central fact is simpler: the administration reportedly possesses the forces and operational machinery to widen the conflict. Everyone else quoted is describing the consequences of power they do not control.

An election is not a legal authorization

The most damning element is the reported timing. CNN’s account, as summarized by AlterNet, says Trump intended to escalate after the midterms, when electoral consequences would be less immediate. If accurate, that makes the election a scheduling constraint on war-making—not a democratic mandate for it.

The report does not establish exactly what legal authority the administration would claim, and Murphy’s warning about the rule of law is a prediction rather than a disclosed legal analysis. Still, postponing a consequential military decision until voters have less leverage would reveal a governing logic in which public accountability is treated as an obstacle to maneuver around.

“Winning” conceals the actual stakes

The framing of a plan to “win” the war launders an enormous burden of proof. The reporting identifies no attainable political objective, no defined end state and no explanation of how broader attacks would produce either. Murphy explicitly said the plan would fail to achieve its objectives, while Mearsheimer argued that Washington had no available route to regain leverage.

Meanwhile, the foreseeable costs are concrete: another cycle of attacks, potential retaliation against regional infrastructure and possible damage to facilities essential for oil production and drinking water. Those consequences would be imposed by governments and military commands, then endured largely by people who had no role in choosing the escalation.

The coverage leaves crucial gaps

AlterNet’s account is built almost entirely from other reporting and hostile assessments of the administration’s strategy. It offers no direct evidence of the plan, no details from the briefing and no response from the officials accused of preparing it. Those are substantial evidentiary limits, not reasons to dismiss the warning.

But the article also weakens its own case by leaning on electoral speculation and unrelated criticism of Trump’s handling of Russia and Ukraine. That material shifts attention from the question that demands scrutiny: what military action is being prepared, who authorized its preparation, under what law, and with what assessment of civilian and regional consequences?

War power thrives on withheld answers

The larger pattern is executive war-making protected by secrecy, delayed accountability and the vocabulary of strategy. Officials can prepare escalation behind classified briefings while the public receives fragments from legislators, anonymous sources and outside analysts. By the time operational details become visible, the machinery may already be deployed.

That structure rewards the decision-makers and burdens everyone else. The president controls the timetable. Military planners control the operational information. Congress is reduced to scattered warnings unless it uses its own powers. Voters encounter the policy as rumor before an election and consequence afterward. The systemic error is not confusion about who is responsible; it is a political order that lets those preparing war conceal the choice until resisting it becomes harder.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The Terrorist Who Never Had to Apologize: Why Major Kira Nerys Remains Star Trek’s Most Politically Courageous Character
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
