item.title: Trump lives in a world of 'total delusion' to fill his 'limitless void'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Michael A. Cohen, director of the International Affairs Program at The New School, described President Donald Trump’s rallies as an “ego-stroking exercise” meant to fill what Cohen called a “limitless void.” That is Cohen’s psychological interpretation, not a fact established by the reporting. Six days before the midterm election, Trump traveled to heavily Republican Texas as his popularity reportedly slipped. On Tuesday, he portrayed the war in Iran as an eco
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Michael A. Cohen, director of the International Affairs Program at The New School, described President Donald Trump’s rallies as an “ego-stroking exercise” meant to fill what Cohen called a “limitless void.” That is Cohen’s psychological interpretation, not a fact established by the reporting.

Six days before the midterm election, Trump traveled to heavily Republican Texas as his popularity reportedly slipped. On Tuesday, he portrayed the war in Iran as an economic windfall and discussed naming the Strait of Hormuz after himself. On Wednesday’s “Daily Blast” podcast, Cohen and host Greg Sargent argued that these remarks showed a president mistaking affirmation from loyal rally audiences for broader public approval.

AlterNet says Cohen characterized the trip as Republican electoral “triage” and faulted Trump for focusing on personal projects, grievances, and rivals instead of issues affecting voters. The article provides no response from Trump or the White House and no polling, economic data, or audience research substantiating its larger conclusions.

The power is presidential

The consequential fact is not whether Trump feels empty. It is that a president can direct the executive branch, shape war policy, command public attention, and use the office’s machinery to turn personal fixations into national business.

That power makes the reported remarks more than rally eccentricity. Trump was presenting a war as proof of prosperity and proposing his own name for a strategic waterway. Even if neither claim became policy, the presidency gave both an institutional platform while Republicans reportedly deployed him to protect their electoral position.

Psychology obscures responsibility

Cohen’s “limitless void” diagnosis is vivid but unverifiable. It also shrinks a political problem into a personality profile. No outsider needs access to Trump’s soul to evaluate the conduct AlterNet describes.

The observable choices are sufficient: Trump chose self-celebration, territorial symbolism, political retaliation, and branding. Republican officials, meanwhile, continued treating his rallies as campaign assets. The relevant agency lies in those decisions—not in speculative explanations about an inner emptiness the article cannot prove.

Loyalty as a feedback system

Sargent’s stronger point concerns the structure surrounding Trump. A rally assembled from committed supporters is not a representative sample of the country. Treating applause there as national consent creates a closed loop: loyalists validate the leader, and the leader cites their validation as evidence of success.

But the loop is not self-sustaining. Party strategists schedule the appearances. Officials repeat the claims. Friendly audiences supply the spectacle. Political institutions convert affirmation into authority. Trump holds the greatest power in that arrangement, while Republican actors enable the system because they expect electoral benefit from it—even when, as Cohen argued, the campaign has been reduced to shoring up a narrowing base.

The missing ledger

AlterNet’s framing leaves the most important claims underdeveloped. If Trump said the Iran war was making Americans rich, the political question is what evidence supported that assertion and who bore the war’s costs. The article supplies neither an economic accounting nor details about the conflict’s consequences.

A weak claim should be tested against material results, not answered mainly with amateur psychoanalysis. By centering Trump’s alleged delusion, the story risks making governance look like one man’s confusion rather than a chain of choices enabled by advisers, party officials, and institutions with the capacity to resist or amplify him.

A system built around the leader

The larger pattern is personalization of public power. Policy becomes autobiography, geography becomes branding, war becomes a campaign testimonial, and the presidency becomes a stage on which loyalty substitutes for evidence.

That system does not require proving Trump’s private motives. It requires powerful people deciding that his desires deserve institutional expression and that their own interests are served by indulging them. The void that matters politically is not inside one man. It is the absence of restraint among those empowered to say no.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: It's not about golf: Trump's latest defiance exposes an 'extraordinary' assault
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump said his administration would proceed with the planned Nov. 15 closure of Washington’s East Potomac Golf Course despite a federal judge’s order restricting further development. Judge Ana C. Reyes extended an injunction and required the government to provide 10 days’ notice before making irreversible changes to the federally owned park. The dispute followed the removal of more than 400 trees. Reyes wrote that conflicting accounts from Tru
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump said his administration would proceed with the planned Nov. 15 closure of Washington’s East Potomac Golf Course despite a federal judge’s order restricting further development. Judge Ana C. Reyes extended an injunction and required the government to provide 10 days’ notice before making irreversible changes to the federally owned park.

The dispute followed the removal of more than 400 trees. Reyes wrote that conflicting accounts from Trump, government employees, and Justice Department attorneys had forced the court to examine whether officials had complied with her earlier orders. Residents and a preservation group brought the lawsuit seeking to preserve the park and its existing public course.

Trump attacked Reyes’s knowledge of golf and claimed she lacked constitutional authority to require notice. AlterNet’s central claim is that the confrontation is not fundamentally about course design: it is about whether the executive branch will accept judicial supervision when pursuing the president’s preferred project.

The power is federal

The residents challenging the redevelopment can sue, and Reyes can issue orders, but the machinery capable of transforming the land belongs to the executive branch. The Interior Department controls the project. Justice Department lawyers represent the government. Federal employees and contractors can close the course, deploy equipment, alter pathways, and remove trees.

That imbalance matters. The preservation plaintiffs did not produce the confrontation by objecting. They invoked the legal mechanism available to people facing an administration with control over public land and the resources to change it irreversibly.

The decision has an owner

Trump publicly claimed the redevelopment as his project and declared that the closure would proceed. Interior officials and government lawyers are therefore not incidental characters. They are the people positioned to execute, enable, explain, or restrain that decision.

Reyes’s order reflects the practical problem: judicial review becomes meaningless if officials complete irreversible work before challengers or the court can respond. Her notice requirement does not design a golf course. It preserves the court’s ability to adjudicate the dispute before the government destroys the subject of it.

Golf is the diversion

Trump’s focus on Reyes’s golf expertise shifts attention from the question she actually confronted: whether the government obeyed court orders and gave accurate accounts of its conduct. A judge does not need to know how to shape a putting green to determine whether executive officials complied with an injunction.

AlterNet is right to reject that diversion, but its own rhetoric occasionally outruns its evidence. The reporting establishes conflicting sworn accounts, sharp judicial criticism, and an announced intention to proceed with the closure. It does not establish what happened after the article was published, whether Trump ultimately violated the extended order, or whether any contempt finding followed.

Defiance depends on enablers

Personalizing the episode around Trump captures who demanded the project, but it can obscure how presidential defiance becomes government action. A social-media declaration cannot fell a tree. Agencies, attorneys, employees, and contractors must translate it into physical and legal reality.

The larger institutional failure begins when those actors treat loyalty to a presidential preference as superior to candor before a court. Reyes described “different accounts,” not a settled finding that every official deliberately deceived her. Even so, a government whose representations cannot be reliably reconciled with its conduct forces judges to supervise routine compliance as though anticipating an ambush.

The systemic error

The golf course is politically revealing precisely because the stakes are smaller than in disputes over detention, health, or civil rights. No emergency rationale is required here. The pattern is executive power pursuing a personal priority, dismissing legal restraint as illegitimate inconvenience, and daring other institutions to stop irreversible action in time.

Courts possess authority, but executive agencies possess the equipment, personnel, and capacity to create facts on the ground. When an administration exploits that gap, law becomes a race against demolition. The trees are not merely scenery in that contest. They demonstrate the consequence of power acting first and treating accountability as paperwork to be argued over afterward.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: 'Absolute immunity’ under fire as new plan hatches to hold Trump accountable
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that former deputy U.S. solicitor general Philip Allen Lacovara condemned the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling as constitutionally unsound and argued that it gives President Donald Trump “a virtual get-out-of-jail card.” He told New York Times contributor Thomas B. Edsall that the decision’s supposed exceptions for some official acts and all unofficial conduct are largely unusable while the Court’s current majority remains intact. The report does n
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former deputy U.S. solicitor general Philip Allen Lacovara condemned the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling as constitutionally unsound and argued that it gives President Donald Trump “a virtual get-out-of-jail card.” He told New York Times contributor Thomas B. Edsall that the decision’s supposed exceptions for some official acts and all unofficial conduct are largely unusable while the Court’s current majority remains intact.

The report does not identify a new plan to hold Trump accountable. It presents Lacovara’s legal criticism and historian Luke Nichter’s broader argument that presidential policymaking, judicial intervention, and congressional passivity have scrambled the constitutional roles of the three branches. AlterNet also connects Trump’s interest in rehabilitating Richard Nixon to supporters’ portrayal of the Watergate prosecution as partisan “lawfare.”

The headline promises more than the reporting delivers

The headline advertises an emerging accountability mechanism. The article supplies none: no legislation, lawsuit, prosecutorial strategy, constitutional amendment, or pending institutional action. Lacovara describes why accountability may be exceptionally difficult; he does not unveil a way around the ruling.

That distinction matters. Turning a severe institutional barrier into the suggestion that some corrective plan is already “hatching” substitutes suspense for substance. The reporting’s actual conclusion is harsher: the institutions empowered to constrain presidential abuse have either fortified executive immunity or declined to exercise their own authority.

Power sits with the Court and the presidency

Trump holds the executive power at issue, but the Supreme Court’s majority established the legal protection surrounding its use. According to Lacovara, the 2024 ruling created an extraordinarily high barrier to prosecuting a president for official conduct and sharply limited the practical value of its nominal exceptions.

Congress also retains substantial constitutional authority. Nichter’s account depicts it surrendering initiative—holding hearings and talking while the president governs through executive action and courts increasingly determine the permissible boundaries. That is not institutional confusion. It is a distribution of choices: executive expansion, judicial permission and legislative retreat.

Accountability cannot survive as a slogan

Lacovara warns that the ruling may obstruct prosecution even where evidence appears to show presidential favors exchanged for financial benefits. His list of potentially insulated abuses includes corruption, election interference, pardon-selling and federal contracts awarded to donors. These are his legal conclusions, not findings that Trump committed each listed act.

The political consequence is nevertheless concrete. A legal system that recognizes presidential criminal liability in theory while making prosecution nearly impossible in practice preserves the language of accountability after draining it of force. “Absolute immunity” need not be formally declared if the evidentiary and procedural barriers produce nearly the same result.

Nixon’s rehabilitation serves executive power

The effort to recast Nixon’s prosecution as Democratic “lawfare” does more than polish one disgraced president’s reputation. It attacks the legitimacy of the historical precedent showing that presidential power can encounter criminal investigation and forced political accountability.

That revision serves the present. If Watergate becomes persecution rather than evidence of executive abuse, then investigation itself can be portrayed as illegitimate whenever it reaches a president. The stronger office becomes the aggrieved party; prosecutors, courts, legislators, and critics become the alleged aggressors. Power is rewritten as victimhood.

A system can fail through permission

The larger pattern is not simply an ambitious president overwhelming helpless institutions. AlterNet’s own evidence describes institutions with agency: Supreme Court justices made the immunity ruling, presidents choose executive action, and members of Congress choose whether to legislate, investigate effectively, or accept marginalization.

Constitutional breakdown rarely requires every formal safeguard to disappear. It can proceed through doctrines that preserve exceptions too narrow to use, hearings that replace consequences, and headlines that imply remedies the reporting cannot identify. The system still performs accountability rhetorically while its most powerful actors make accountability materially harder.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Seth Meyers mocks Trump’s cognitive abilities after bizarre claim
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Seth Meyers mocked President Donald Trump after Trump told reporters, following early voting in Florida on an unspecified Saturday, that his uncle John G. Trump “invented radar.” The article says John G. Trump was a respected MIT professor who worked on radar during World War II but did not invent it. Meyers used the false claim to ridicule Trump’s repeated boasts about passing cognitive tests. Meyers also targeted two campaign spectacles described by AlterNet
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Seth Meyers mocked President Donald Trump after Trump told reporters, following early voting in Florida on an unspecified Saturday, that his uncle John G. Trump “invented radar.” The article says John G. Trump was a respected MIT professor who worked on radar during World War II but did not invent it. Meyers used the false claim to ridicule Trump’s repeated boasts about passing cognitive tests.

Meyers also targeted two campaign spectacles described by AlterNet: Republican congressional candidate Joe Mitchell presenting Trump with a self-created “Man of the Century” award in Iowa, and Trump proposing at a Florida rally that New Mexico be renamed “New America.” The article says these appearances renewed questions about Trump’s mental fitness, but it supplies no medical evidence or expert assessment establishing cognitive impairment.

The power is not on late-night television

Meyers has a platform, an audience and a joke writer’s ability to puncture vanity. Trump has presidential authority. That distinction matters more than the monologue.

The consequential fact is not that a comedian found the remarks absurd. It is that a president made a plainly false historical claim while speaking publicly, then continued through a campaign environment built to applaud him. Institutional power belongs to Trump and to the political apparatus that promotes, excuses or launders his statements—not to the host describing the performance.

Flattery as political infrastructure

The invented award is more revealing than its cheap appearance. According to AlterNet, Mitchell created it and then bestowed it on Trump. That makes the episode an act of political ingratiation, not an achievement being recognized.

Mitchell exercised agency: he manufactured a distinction and presented it to the most powerful figure in his party’s orbit. Trump accepted the spectacle. The exchange shows how political subordinates can convert deference into campaign theater, supplying the leader with symbolic triumphs when reality does not cooperate.

Diagnosis is a distraction

AlterNet frames the remarks as evidence renewing concern about Trump’s cognitive fitness and adds speculation about his physical appearance. But the article offers neither a diagnosis nor evidence connecting appearance to incapacity. That framing is weak because it turns observable conduct into amateur medicine.

No diagnosis is necessary to assess what happened. Trump made a false claim about his uncle. A Republican candidate fabricated an award for him. Trump floated an incoherent renaming of New Mexico. Those are political facts involving judgment, truthfulness and a culture of sycophancy. Treating them principally as symptoms risks converting accountable behavior into an involuntary condition—and lets the officials enabling it disappear from view.

The permission structure

The larger pattern is an ecosystem in which falsehood and flattery carry little internal cost. A president can invent family history, while an allied candidate invents an honor for the president. One fiction magnifies personal genius; the other manufactures public acclaim. Both move in the same direction: power receives affirmation instead of correction.

Late-night ridicule can expose the absurdity, but it cannot impose institutional consequences. The sharper question is not whether Trump can pass a test he boasts about passing. It is why people seeking power through him have an incentive to reward his claims, stage his validation and leave correction to comedians.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Life-saving disaster relief sabotaged by right-wing trolls
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet’s publication of Grist’s reporting shows how false disaster claims obstructed relief after the 2023 Maui wildfires and Hurricane Helene in 2024. Right-wing influencers and other social-media accounts spread unsupported allegations about energy weapons, government land seizures, withheld aid, and FEMA interference. During Helene, a reported armed threat forced FEMA to suspend North Carolina field operations for several hours; anonymous callers also prompted police SWAT depl
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet’s publication of Grist’s reporting shows how false disaster claims obstructed relief after the 2023 Maui wildfires and Hurricane Helene in 2024. Right-wing influencers and other social-media accounts spread unsupported allegations about energy weapons, government land seizures, withheld aid, and FEMA interference. During Helene, a reported armed threat forced FEMA to suspend North Carolina field operations for several hours; anonymous callers also prompted police SWAT deployments at the homes of FEMA leaders.

The reporting traces one supposed image of a Maui “laser” to a 2018 refinery flare in Ohio. Although the account that misidentified it later apologized, another account’s video repeating the falsehood received 432,000 views—more than 40 times the apology’s audience. Elon Musk’s unsupported accusation that FEMA blocked his aid flights drew almost 30 million views; his walk-back drew about 1 million.

The precise human toll cannot be calculated from the reporting. Former FEMA administrator Deanne Criswell said there is no way to know how many Maui residents avoided assistance because of the rumors. But disrupted fieldwork, diverted emergency resources, and fear of applying for aid created obvious risks for people who needed shelter and support.

The saboteurs had names

“Misinformation” is too bloodless when prominent accounts use institutional distrust as engagement bait. End Wokeness accused President Biden of starving North Carolina of aid without evidence. Musk broadcast his FEMA allegation to an enormous audience before retreating from it. Charlie Kirk and other right-wing personalities amplified Maui conspiracy claims. These were choices made by people with platforms, not weather-generated confusion.

The reporting does not establish that every person sharing a falsehood knew it was false. Some apparently believed what they circulated, and accounts linked to China also promoted Maui rumors. That distinction matters when judging intent. It does not erase agency: influential publishers chose to broadcast extraordinary accusations without adequate verification, and their reach magnified the foreseeable damage.

Platforms hold the machinery

Individual trolls supplied the content, but social-media companies supplied the distribution system. Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and X possess the institutional power to rank, recommend, label, and restrict posts. According to the reporting, major platforms have retreated from serious fact-checking and moderation while verified accounts produce much of the conspiracy material.

That structure rewards accusation over correction. The false claim reaches millions while the retraction limps behind it. Treating this as an unfortunate feature of human psychology misdirects attention from companies that design and govern the amplification machinery. Users press “share”; platforms decide how far the result travels.

Distrust is being weaponized

Fear of government does not arise from one source. Native Hawaiians carry legitimate historical memories of colonization, while undocumented residents may reasonably fear state scrutiny. Disaster propagandists exploit those vulnerabilities by attaching invented plots to real institutional trauma—such as the false warning that FEMA would seize Maui applicants’ homes.

That is not skepticism serving accountability. It redirects scrutiny away from documented failures and toward fantasies that make public assistance itself appear dangerous. The result benefits political actors seeking to portray government as inherently predatory, even when government workers are delivering shelter, benefits, and emergency information.

The article’s broad language about a fragmented “information landscape” risks blurring that asymmetry. Confusion is the environment; powerful accounts and permissive platforms are the actors exploiting it.

A weakened state pays twice

Emergency agencies must now perform two jobs at once: respond to the disaster and defend the legitimacy of responding. Every hour spent rebutting laser stories, investigating threats, or suspending field operations is capacity unavailable for relief. Staffing reductions described in the reporting make that burden heavier.

FEMA’s partnerships with a Native Hawaiian employee, caregivers, and other locally trusted messengers were a practical response. But community trust cannot substitute for platform accountability or sufficient public staffing. Forcing emergency workers to out-organize viral falsehoods one relationship at a time leaves the state permanently on the defensive.

Disaster politics by attrition

The larger pattern is institutional sabotage without the need to abolish an institution. Flood the public sphere with claims that FEMA steals land, blocks aid, or serves a secret plot; provoke threats and operational delays; then point to strained relief as proof that government cannot function.

The reporting cannot quantify every lost application, delayed placement, or endangered resident. It establishes something more basic: false claims consumed attention, interrupted operations, and made assistance harder to trust. In an era of worsening climate disasters, that machinery does not merely degrade debate. It turns political propaganda and platform incentives into additional hazards for people already trying to survive.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Even her right-wing pals think this Trump insider is pushing things too far
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, republishing ProPublica’s reporting, identifies conservative election lawyer Cleta Mitchell as the Trump insider whose escalation alarms even some allies. In July, Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network received a private White House briefing before President Donald Trump delivered an address repeating election allegations promoted by her network and urging Congress to pass proof-of-citizenship legislation she helped draft. Mitchell holds no administration post, but allies
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, republishing ProPublica’s reporting, identifies conservative election lawyer Cleta Mitchell as the Trump insider whose escalation alarms even some allies. In July, Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network received a private White House briefing before President Donald Trump delivered an address repeating election allegations promoted by her network and urging Congress to pass proof-of-citizenship legislation she helped draft.

Mitchell holds no administration post, but allies told ProPublica she has frequent White House access. Her associates have obtained election-related positions in swing states and the administration, while officials close to her have pursued alleged noncitizen voting and revisited purported 2020 irregularities. Mitchell denies seeking to sway election outcomes and says her work is intended to make elections accurate and transparent.

Some conservatives told ProPublica that Mitchell’s frustration with legislative and judicial setbacks is driving increasingly aggressive proposals. After Trump’s address, Steve Bannon suggested declaring a national emergency; Mitchell argued Trump could instead invoke existing critical-infrastructure authority to impose requirements resembling those in the stalled SAVE America Act. The reporting does not establish that the administration adopted her theory.

The power is in the White House

Mitchell has influence, money, personnel and a network built to penetrate election administration. But the constitutional and coercive power belongs to Trump and the officials he appoints. Only the administration can turn her proposals into federal investigations, demands for voter data or attempted executive mandates.

Calling Mitchell a rogue outsider would therefore obscure the essential arrangement. The White House briefed her organization alongside governors, members of Congress and major news outlets. Her claims appeared in a presidential address. Her associates entered government. Whatever her formal title, the administration chose to give her project access and reach.

This was built, not stumbled into

ProPublica describes years of deliberate institution-building: fundraising, litigation, model legislation, local organizing and recruitment into election posts. After Trump’s 2020 defeat, Mitchell did not merely continue arguing about one election. She created the Election Integrity Network and trained supporters to master election rules, work at polling places and seek seats on local boards.

That infrastructure matters more than Mitchell’s inflammatory rhetoric. Claims that the 2020 election was stolen and that noncitizen voting is rampant became organizing premises, then policy proposals, then material for a presidential speech. A political narrative acquired lawyers, donors, activists and government personnel. That is how a fringe campaign becomes governing capacity.

The “too far” frame misdirects

The headline’s focus on right-wing discomfort offers a misleading measure of severity. Conservative allies becoming uneasy does not create the danger; it merely shows that Mitchell’s preferred tactics may now exceed what some participants consider legally defensible or politically useful.

Nor is this primarily a story about one operative’s obsession. Trump welcomed Mitchell’s assistance in contesting his 2020 loss, repeated claims associated with her network and staffed his administration with people connected to her project. Senate Republicans and courts blocked parts of the agenda, but those checks do not erase the choices made by the officials who advanced it.

The framing also risks treating escalation as personal frustration. ProPublica’s own evidence shows continuity: Mitchell urged planning before the 2020 election to dispute possible results, joined Trump’s call pressuring Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, recruited John Eastman to produce a constitutional memo and later built a national election network. Mitchell disputes that she sought to overturn the election and denies responsibility for Eastman’s subsequent advice. Even with those denials preserved, escalation is not a new mood. It is the method described throughout the reporting.

Suspicion as an instrument

Mitchell has said Democrats “only win when they cheat” and characterized resistance to her agenda as opposition to honest elections. That formulation makes contrary evidence nearly useless: defeat proves cheating, resistance proves corruption, and institutional limits become evidence that institutions cannot be trusted.

The practical consequence is a self-sealing justification for tighter registration rules, voter-roll challenges and greater federal intervention. A debunked claim about more than 275,000 noncitizens on state voter rolls still reached a presidential address, according to ProPublica. The political utility lies not only in proving misconduct, but in manufacturing enough suspicion to justify new control over who registers, whose eligibility is challenged and which level of government dictates election procedures.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of election denial into administrative policy. A private advocate develops claims and legislation; an organizing network supplies personnel; the president supplies executive authority and a national platform. Each part lets the others evade full responsibility.

Mitchell can say she holds no office. The White House can call her merely an effective advocate. Republican officials can portray restrictive measures as technical safeguards. But institutional power is visible in the chain connecting her network to presidential rhetoric, federal appointments and proposed control over state election systems.

The central issue is not whether Mitchell has finally gone “too far” for some allies. It is that powerful officials repeatedly moved her ideas closer to state action—and could do so precisely because years of organized election suspicion had already made extraordinary intervention look, within the movement, like ordinary governance.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump's unusually small venue stuns veteran reporter
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that NBC News correspondent Garrett Haake was surprised by the unusually small venue chosen for Donald Trump’s Wednesday rally in Chillicothe, Ohio. Haake said the Ohio University athletic facility might hold about 1,000 people—smaller than any Trump rally space he could recall after covering “dozens if not hundreds” of them. The event was presented as an effort to boost Republican candidates Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy ahead of the following week’s midterm elec
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that NBC News correspondent Garrett Haake was surprised by the unusually small venue chosen for Donald Trump’s Wednesday rally in Chillicothe, Ohio. Haake said the Ohio University athletic facility might hold about 1,000 people—smaller than any Trump rally space he could recall after covering “dozens if not hundreds” of them.

The event was presented as an effort to boost Republican candidates Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy ahead of the following week’s midterm elections. Citing Mediaite and Axios, AlterNet reported that Ramaswamy had fallen further behind Democrat Amy Acton in internal polling after an attack ad involving Acton’s estranged mother drew bipartisan criticism. The supplied reporting was published before the rally and does not establish its final attendance or effect.

The room is not the power

A smaller arena may indicate lowered expectations, tactical caution, local constraints, or weakening enthusiasm. The reporting does not establish which explanation is correct. Treating venue capacity alone as proof of Trump’s political decline would turn a suggestive detail into an unsupported conclusion.

Trump’s institutional importance here comes from his ability to direct attention, activate partisan media, and confer standing on Republican candidates. A 1,000-person room does not erase that leverage. The operative fact is that candidates in statewide races were still being positioned to receive his endorsement and audience.

Republicans made the choices

Husted and Ramaswamy were not passive objects caught in Trump’s gravitational field. Their campaigns—and the Republican organizations supporting them—made strategic choices about candidates, messages, and alliances.

The clearest reported electoral damage concerns Ramaswamy’s own campaign. According to Axios, Republicans feared that his personal attack involving Acton’s estranged mother could cost them the governor’s race, while internal polling reportedly showed Acton widening her lead. That is agency, not confusion: a campaign selected an attack, aired it, and then confronted a backlash.

Spectacle displaces accountability

The venue provides an irresistible visual shorthand: the former stadium act reduced to something critics compared to a school gym. But crowd-size mockery can misdirect attention from the people exercising power and the decisions shaping the races.

Even Trump’s reported comments about examining Husted’s body—crude remarks that Mediaite said he had repeated—risk becoming another piece of spectacle detached from consequence. The political question is not whether the performance is dignified. It is why Republican candidates continue treating the performer as a valuable campaign asset despite the degradation and distraction he brings with him.

The shrinking-stage trap

Political journalism often substitutes optics for measurement. Room size is easy to photograph; organizational control, donor influence, party discipline, and candidate dependence are harder to compress into a post. The result is coverage that can mistake a diminished stage for diminished power.

The larger pattern is a party ecosystem organized around attention rather than accountability. Candidates seek Trump’s imprimatur, journalists track the scale of his crowds, and campaign decisions disappear behind the traveling show. The venue may have been unusually small. The machinery that made him central to these Ohio races was not.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: 'Saw' director: Hollywood is shy about Trump content — and that's scary
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that director Kevin Greutert believes studios and financiers avoid explicit Trump-era political stories because they fear alienating “half of the American body politic.” He said that concern killed The Endorsement , a proposed horror film about a small-town journalist threatened by a politically motivated serial killer after persuading her newspaper to endorse Hillary Clinton in 2016. Greutert also said a planned version of Saw XI involving two mayoral candidates a
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that director Kevin Greutert believes studios and financiers avoid explicit Trump-era political stories because they fear alienating “half of the American body politic.” He said that concern killed The Endorsement, a proposed horror film about a small-town journalist threatened by a politically motivated serial killer after persuading her newspaper to endorse Hillary Clinton in 2016.

Greutert also said a planned version of Saw XI involving two mayoral candidates and an election-themed trap was abandoned when “a different approach was selected,” though he did not say political pressure caused that decision. He contrasted those experiences with Saw VI, whose attack on health-insurance power reached theaters in 2009 partly, he suggested, because producers had not anticipated how politically charged healthcare reform would become.

In the interview, Greutert condemned the killing attributed to Luigi Mangione and rejected political violence. He also argued that horror can expose abusive power through stories of captivity, exploitation and helplessness, even when filmmakers avoid naming contemporary politicians directly.

The veto belongs to capital

The decisive actors here are not moviegoers imagined as two equally sized, permanently offended camps. They are studio executives, producers and financiers who control which scripts receive money, distribution and an audience.

According to Greutert, those gatekeepers rejected The Endorsement because explicit political content might repel part of the market. That is not public censorship, and the interview does not establish government coercion behind the decision. It is private capital exercising cultural power through risk avoidance.

The distinction matters. “Hollywood is shy” turns an institutional choice into a personality trait, as though an industry became bashful. Executives made—or declined to make—specific investments. Their caution protects revenue and access; its consequence is a narrower political imagination on screen.

Neutrality for sale

The demand not to “offend half” sounds like fairness only if every political subject is treated as an interchangeable consumer preference. A story about intimidation following a newspaper endorsement is not merely partisan branding. It concerns whether threats can punish political speech.

Yet the financing logic Greutert describes converts that conflict into market segmentation. The aggressor, the target and the institution capable of protecting expression disappear into a spreadsheet labeled “controversy.” This is how commercial neutrality launders power: the powerful retain their capacity to intimidate, while artists are told that naming the conflict would itself be divisive.

Ambiguity can produce excellent art. Greutert points to Invasion of the Body Snatchers and The Twilight Zone as works that used genre to approach politics indirectly. But creative indirection and compulsory evasiveness are not the same thing. One expands meaning; the other limits what can be financed.

Where the interview overreaches

AlterNet’s strongest evidence concerns Greutert’s own projects and what he says financiers told his team. Its broader claims are considerably less secure. The interviewer asserts that Trump allies are purchasing media companies and that the government has tried to stifle critical comedians, but the supplied article does not substantiate those claims.

Greutert also speculates that Trump, given the opportunity, would treat political opponents as Augusto Pinochet’s regime did. That is an opinion and a hypothetical, not a reported act or established plan. Presenting it alongside concrete accounts of rejected film projects risks substituting analogy for evidence.

The article’s political framing is therefore uneven. It identifies a real gatekeeping mechanism, then dilutes that finding with claims it does not document. Scathing conclusions require stronger sourcing, not louder comparisons.

Horror knows who controls the room

Greutert’s most useful observation is simpler: horror is often organized around unequal power. Someone controls the basement, the trap, the institution or the terms of escape. Someone else bears the pain. That structure can illuminate politics because politics also determines who may impose costs and who is forced to absorb them.

But the language of universal helplessness can blur responsibility. Greutert says audiences are implicated in systems from which they benefit, yet shared participation does not mean equal agency. A consumer, a filmmaker and a studio executive do not possess the same ability to decide what gets produced. Nor does a patient denied coverage wield the power of the executive administering the policy.

The sharper political horror story is not that everyone is trapped. It is that identifiable institutions build the trap, authorized decision-makers maintain it, and weaker people are then blamed for failing to escape.

The system prefers a monster without a name

This episode reveals how cultural institutions domesticate political art. They may tolerate injustice as metaphor, corruption as atmosphere and authoritarianism as an unnamed monster. What alarms them is specificity: a recognizable election, an identifiable movement, a conflict whose beneficiaries cannot pretend the story concerns somebody else.

No censor needs to issue an order when concentrated financing already rewards ambiguity and penalizes confrontation. The result is not silence, exactly. It is an industry permitted to depict terror while remaining coy about who holds the keys.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Jeanine Pirro threw FBI director under the bus in new case he demanded
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt testified at a Tuesday hearing that FBI Director Kash Patel personally directed an investigation of agents Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides. Witt said the July assignment, routed through the Kansas City field office, was unlike any tasking he had received from an FBI director during his career. Defense questioning also exposed serious weaknesses in the resulting case. Witt acknowledged that neither agent had been sworn to tell th
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt testified at a Tuesday hearing that FBI Director Kash Patel personally directed an investigation of agents Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides. Witt said the July assignment, routed through the Kansas City field office, was unlike any tasking he had received from an FBI director during his career.

Defense questioning also exposed serious weaknesses in the resulting case. Witt acknowledged that neither agent had been sworn to tell the truth, despite his affidavit saying they were, and that House Judiciary Committee counsel Steve Castor was absent from the interviews in which the alleged false statements were made. Witt had spoken with Castor only the day before the hearing, and the Justice Department declined to disclose Castor’s knowledge, citing the Speech or Debate Clause.

The headline’s claim that Jeanine Pirro “threw” Patel under the bus is not established by the reporting. The damaging attribution came from Witt’s testimony: Patel ordered the investigation. Pirro’s role, as presented by AlterNet through national security writer Marcy Wheeler’s analysis, was in pursuing charges that gave defense lawyers an opportunity to expose how the case originated.

Power ordered the case

Floris and Benavides did not choose this confrontation. Patel held the institutional power to initiate an extraordinary investigation from the top of the FBI, and Witt carried out the assignment through the chain of command. The unusual feature was not merely bureaucratic untidiness. It was the director’s direct intervention in a case targeting agents whose 2020 work included resisting foreign election interference.

That distinction matters because “the FBI investigated” conceals agency. According to the testimony AlterNet recounts, Patel directed it. Career personnel then inherited the legal and professional risk created by that decision.

The case weakened under examination

The government’s theory depended on alleged false statements to a congressional committee. Yet its investigating agent lacked direct knowledge of what the committee’s counsel considered material, had only just spoken with Castor, and admitted a basic factual error in his own affidavit about whether Floris and Benavides testified under oath.

An inaccurate affidavit does not by itself prove intentional deception. It does, however, expose a glaring asymmetry: officials were attempting to criminalize alleged inaccuracies by the defendants while presenting their own inaccurate description to the court. A prosecution built around truthfulness cannot treat precision as optional when the government supplies it.

The headline obscures the chain of command

Casting this as Pirro betraying Patel turns an institutional abuse story into palace intrigue. The consequential fact is not that one Trump official embarrassed another. It is that the FBI director allegedly initiated an unusual investigation, prosecutors advanced a defective complaint, and the Justice Department invoked a constitutional protection that limited scrutiny of a congressional staff member central to its theory.

That framing redirects attention from state power toward personality conflict. Floris and Benavides face the coercive machinery of federal prosecution; Patel, Pirro, and senior Justice Department officials control that machinery. Those positions are not interchangeable, and the reporting should not flatten them into a spectacle of allies “throwing” one another around.

Criminalization as discipline

Wheeler argues that the case sought to make rejecting frivolous election-fraud claims legally dangerous inside the FBI. The hearing does not independently prove that motive, but the reported sequence supports scrutiny of it: Patel personally ordered an unusual inquiry into agents associated with protecting the 2020 election, and the resulting case faltered when tested against its own evidence.

The foreseeable message to other agents is plain. Professional judgment can become personal exposure when it conflicts with the political leadership’s preferred account. Even a weak case can punish through legal fees, reputational damage and the threat of prosecution.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of law enforcement hierarchy into a channel for political retaliation, followed by procedural language that disguises who exercised power. Orders become “taskings.” Political choices become ordinary casework. Evidentiary defects become confusion.

This hearing disrupted that laundering process. It placed the director’s instruction, the investigators’ omissions and the prosecutors’ choices into the same record. The scandal is not that the officials involved failed to coordinate their stories cleanly. It is that federal authority was reportedly mobilized against agents tied to election-protection work—and that the case’s internal weaknesses emerged only after the targets had already been forced to defend themselves.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: MAGA 'party girl' flailing amid scandal avalanche and Trump's ire
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, summarizing an Intelligencer profile by Jake Lahut, reports that Rep. Lauren Boebert entered the 2026 midterm campaign facing a closer-than-expected race, several personal and political controversies, and uncertainty about Donald Trump’s support. Her challenger, retired Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, is seeking to unseat her; Boebert has attacked Laubacher as a “Deep State Dem” and linked her to progressive politics. The reported controversies include the August arrest
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing an Intelligencer profile by Jake Lahut, reports that Rep. Lauren Boebert entered the 2026 midterm campaign facing a closer-than-expected race, several personal and political controversies, and uncertainty about Donald Trump’s support. Her challenger, retired Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, is seeking to unseat her; Boebert has attacked Laubacher as a “Deep State Dem” and linked her to progressive politics.

The reported controversies include the August arrest of Boebert’s 21-year-old son on charges of sexual exploitation of a child and a House Ethics Committee complaint from critic David Wheeler alleging that Boebert had sexual relationships with staffers. The profile does not establish the truth of Wheeler’s allegations or report a committee finding. Boebert responded by saying she is neither lesbian nor bisexual.

The profile also reports tension with Trump’s political operation because Boebert supported releasing the Epstein files. Trump threatened earlier in the year to withdraw his endorsement after she campaigned with Rep. Thomas Massie, but did not do so. According to Lahut, Boebert is the last of four House Republicans who advanced the Epstein vote who remained headed toward Election Day.

Scandal is not a unit of measurement

Calling this an “avalanche” collapses events of radically different meaning into one marketable pile. A criminal charge against Boebert’s adult son is not evidence of misconduct by Boebert. An ethics complaint against her is an allegation, not a finding. Her position on releasing the Epstein files is a political decision, not a personal scandal.

That distinction matters because scandal coverage often substitutes accumulation for proof. If enough adverse facts and allegations are stacked together, the politician appears convicted by atmosphere. Boebert’s record deserves scrutiny, but scrutiny requires separating her conduct from her relatives’ conduct and substantiated findings from accusations.

The power sits above the spectacle

The consequential actor here is not a Democratic critic enjoying Boebert’s difficulties. It is Trump, whose endorsement and political network can shape a Republican incumbent’s survival. His reported threat to withdraw support demonstrated the hierarchy even though he did not carry it out.

Boebert helped force action on the Epstein files and then encountered hostility from the leader of her party. That is the institutional story: loyalty to Trumpworld can be enforced through threatened electoral punishment. The endorsement becomes leverage, and disclosure becomes costly when it conflicts with the leader’s preferences.

The framing points downward

The “party girl” label and emphasis on alleged affairs direct attention toward sex, identity, and humiliation. Wheeler’s complaint may warrant investigation, particularly because it concerns alleged relationships with staffers, where workplace authority could be relevant. But the reporting supplied here provides no ethics finding and no established facts about those alleged relationships.

Highlighting the alleged same-sex dimension because Boebert opposes same-sex marriage may expose hypocrisy if the allegation is substantiated. Before that, it mainly turns sexuality into spectacle. Boebert’s denial of being lesbian or bisexual does not resolve the staff-conduct allegation, and her orientation would not itself be an ethics violation. The sharper question is whether she misused official power—not whether the accusation furnishes an irresistible culture-war punchline.

Voters are not supporting characters

The profile frames Democrats as closing in on a long-held “dream” and recalls Adam Frisch’s 546-vote loss in 2022. But neither Democratic enthusiasm nor Republican resentment decides the seat by itself. Voters do.

Treating the race as a drama of partisan revenge obscures the actual contest: whether Boebert’s constituents approve of her representation, whether Laubacher persuades them, and how national Republican power affects that choice. “Even Republicans” wanting Boebert humbled is colorful anecdote, not a substitute for electoral evidence.

The system rewards obedience and spectacle

This story reveals two reinforcing political habits. Party leaders use endorsements and primary threats to discipline members, while political media packages the resulting struggle as personality collapse. One mechanism exercises power; the other makes the exercise look like gossip.

Boebert’s vulnerability may be real. The supplied reporting does not establish that any single controversy will defeat her, or that Trump’s displeasure caused the departures and defeat of the other Republicans who backed the Epstein vote. What it does establish is a system in which defying a dominant party leader carries visible risk—and coverage can bury that coercive structure beneath a more clickable inventory of personal scandal.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
