item.title: CNN tries to pretend its MAGA scandal 'never happened': report
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Hasan Piker sued CNN contributor Scott Jennings in federal court in Washington, D.C., alleging defamation and seeking $72.5 million in damages. The complaint concerns an August broadcast on Jennings’s Salem radio show, where Jennings said Piker was “calling for Black voters to be lynched.” According to the lawsuit, the underlying clip combined excerpts from three streams and removed context showing that Piker was describing and mocking someone else’s remark. A
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Hasan Piker sued CNN contributor Scott Jennings in federal court in Washington, D.C., alleging defamation and seeking $72.5 million in damages. The complaint concerns an August broadcast on Jennings’s Salem radio show, where Jennings said Piker was “calling for Black voters to be lynched.”

According to the lawsuit, the underlying clip combined excerpts from three streams and removed context showing that Piker was describing and mocking someone else’s remark. AlterNet says the clip circulated through the National Republican Senatorial Committee before Jennings’s program used it. These remain allegations in a pending civil case; the report supplies no ruling on whether Jennings defamed Piker.

Journalist Colby Hall argued that CNN had responded conspicuously: 64 words aggregating Variety in its Reliable Sources newsletter and, at the time of his writing, no on-air coverage. Hall said CNN did not answer his request for comment.

The power is institutional

Piker can sue, deny the accusation and show the omitted context. But Jennings, Salem, CNN and the NRSC occupy the institutions that can convert a manipulated social-media clip into a nationally distributed political claim.

That hierarchy matters. CNN pays Jennings and repeatedly places him inside its news product. Hall’s point is not merely that Jennings appears on the network; it is that CNN has made him a central conservative voice across debates, conventions and major speeches. The network supplies reach, prestige and an implicit judgment that his commentary belongs within legitimate political discussion.

The decisions have names

The lawsuit alleges that Jennings broadcast a grave accusation based on a deceptively edited clip. Salem aired it. The NRSC reportedly circulated the clip. CNN did not make the disputed statement, but it chose to build programming around Jennings and then, according to Hall, largely avoided covering the resulting lawsuit.

Those are separate decisions with different degrees of responsibility. CNN is not automatically liable for what a contributor says on another company’s program. But editorial responsibility is broader than legal liability. A network cannot make a pundit valuable through constant exposure, benefit from his provocations and then treat scrutiny of his conduct as somebody else’s departmental problem.

The scapegoat machine

The political function of the disputed clip was straightforward: turn a left-wing streamer into evidence that Democratic politics harbors extremism. AlterNet describes Republicans using Piker as a boogeyman against Democratic midterm candidates. If the complaint’s account of the editing is accurate, the maneuver was not criticism of what Piker said. It was the manufacture of a more useful thing for him to have said.

That is how scapegoating works in modern campaign media. A weaker actor’s words are stripped of context, recirculated by a party committee and repeated by a credentialed commentator. The accusation then becomes the story, while the institutions that produced and amplified it fade into the background.

Silence is also framing

CNN’s scant treatment, as described by Hall, redirects attention away from its own role. The issue is not that the network must declare Jennings guilty before adjudication. It can report the complaint, describe the allegation, seek responses and state clearly that the case is unresolved. That is routine journalism.

Ignoring the case on air instead creates an asymmetry. Piker can be extensively covered as a political liability for Democrats, while a serious allegation against the CNN personality helping construct that image receives minimal institutional scrutiny. The network’s apparent standard is therefore not simply newsworthiness. It is newsworthiness constrained by self-interest.

The pundit loophole

The larger pattern is a media business model built to harvest provocation while dispersing accountability. Networks hire personalities whose value comes from conflict across television, radio and social platforms. When those personalities generate attention, the network claims the energy. When their outside conduct becomes damaging, it invokes the corporate boundary.

That boundary may matter in court. Politically, it is a loophole. Institutions manufacture authority through repetition and visibility, then pretend that authority disappears whenever responsibility arrives. The result is a system in which inflammatory claims travel at full institutional speed, while corrections, context and accountability are forced to proceed one lawsuit—and one conveniently neglected story—at a time.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The 8 enablers shaking up the DOJ to do Trump's dirty work
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting by Devlin Barrett, identifies eight federal prosecutors who allegedly used Justice Department power to pursue President Donald Trump’s grievances against critics, protesters and officials. The reported targets included Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, former FBI Director James Comey, former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell and people protesting immigration enforcement. According to the account, Dan
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting by Devlin Barrett, identifies eight federal prosecutors who allegedly used Justice Department power to pursue President Donald Trump’s grievances against critics, protesters and officials. The reported targets included Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, former FBI Director James Comey, former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell and people protesting immigration enforcement.

According to the account, Daniel Rosen, John Sarcone III, Dan Bishop, Bill Essayli, Jason Reding Quiñones, Jeanine Pirro, W. Ellis Boyle and Andrew Boutros advanced investigations or charges that repeatedly met resistance from judges, grand jurors and career prosecutors. Some cases collapsed or were dismissed; a judge found Sarcone was not lawfully serving as acting U.S. attorney; and three of the eight reportedly ran their offices without Senate confirmation.

The reporting also says prosecutors who concluded that charges were unwarranted were pushed out, while weak cases consumed federal resources and damaged careers inside the department. Those claims rest here on AlterNet’s account of Barrett’s reporting, court rulings and unnamed people familiar with certain events.

The power runs downward

Trump held the decisive political power described in this story. He publicly or privately identified enemies, demanded action and placed loyal appointees in institutions capable of searching homes, seizing ballots, issuing subpoenas and bringing criminal charges.

The prosecutors still had agency. A presidential demand is not a self-executing indictment. Lawyers chose whether to test evidence, resist pressure or convert a grievance into a federal proceeding. The reported removal of prosecutors who found no basis for charges shows how the system disciplined restraint and rewarded persistence.

Failure is not the same as harmlessness

The record presented by AlterNet is full of failed prosecutions: protest cases collapsing, charges dismissed and subpoenas rejected. That can create the comforting impression that judicial review worked and the danger passed.

But prosecution itself imposes punishment. A target can face a search, legal costs, reputational damage and years of uncertainty before a judge finally says the government lacked evidence. The state does not need to win every case to make opposition expensive.

Thin evidence, heavy machinery

The sharpest example is not merely that judges rejected cases. It is that officials allegedly pressed forward after internal objections or visible evidentiary defects. AlterNet reports that Essayli insisted on charging a man who supplied face shields to anti-ICE protesters despite staff resistance. It also reports that Pirro’s office pursued David Hearn after learning of a significant weakness, according to filings by Hearn’s lawyers.

Those details matter because they strip away the language of bureaucratic confusion. The account describes identifiable officials making discretionary decisions. Where evidence was thin, institutional power remained immense.

The framing understates the system

Calling these officials “enablers” is accurate but incomplete. It can make them sound like secondary characters indulging one man’s impulses. They were reportedly officeholders exercising delegated federal authority, and some did so without the legitimacy ordinarily supplied by Senate confirmation.

The deeper scandal is an incentive structure: loyalty appears to open doors, evidentiary restraint can end careers, and courtroom defeat arrives only after the government has imposed the process. The stronger actors create the pressure; weaker targets absorb the cost. Blaming only Trump’s temperament would conceal the lawyers and institutions that translated it into action.

Personalized justice is still state policy

This story reveals how retaliatory government becomes routine. It does not require every accusation to produce a conviction. It requires officials willing to launch proceedings, supervisors willing to punish resistance and institutions slow enough that eventual dismissal cannot undo the damage.

The systemic error is treating collapsed cases as proof of resilience. They are also evidence that extraordinary coercive power was activated on weak grounds. When professional independence becomes a liability and personal loyalty becomes a qualification, the Justice Department’s failures stop looking accidental. They become the foreseeable output of how power has been organized.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: FBI agents 'worried' about being tools in Trump's power grab: report
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, citing MS NOW, reports that current and former FBI officials fear the Trump administration could use the bureau to seize voting machines, ballots, or other election materials through legally questionable investigations. The officials pointed to prior seizures of state voting records and equipment, including ballots in Fulton County, Georgia, as grounds for concern. According to the report, two Atlanta-based FBI intelligence analysts were fired in July after refusing to wo
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, citing MS NOW, reports that current and former FBI officials fear the Trump administration could use the bureau to seize voting machines, ballots, or other election materials through legally questionable investigations. The officials pointed to prior seizures of state voting records and equipment, including ballots in Fulton County, Georgia, as grounds for concern.

According to the report, two Atlanta-based FBI intelligence analysts were fired in July after refusing to work on an administration investigation into the 2020 election. Former FBI supervisor Rob D’Amico said agents worry the bureau could be used to obtain warrants based on questionable probable cause. Election advocates are reportedly preparing legal and professional support for agents ordered to perform work they consider illegal or unethical.

The power is at the top

The central actors are not anxious rank-and-file agents. Institutional power belongs to the president, Justice Department officials, U.S. attorneys, and FBI leaders who can open investigations, seek warrants, assign personnel, and punish refusal.

That distinction matters. Agents may execute a seizure, but senior officials create the conditions for it: selecting allegations, authorizing investigations, presenting applications to judges, and directing armed federal personnel. The reported firing of two analysts shows why private concern is an inadequate safeguard. An employee who refuses can lose a career; an official issuing the order retains the machinery of the state.

Anxiety is not resistance

The article frames FBI agents as “worried,” but worry neither blocks an improper order nor protects an election. The decisive question is whether officials will refuse legally unsupported assignments, document pressure, alert oversight bodies, or challenge retaliation.

The reported preparations by election advocates recognize this imbalance. Legal assistance can lower the personal cost of refusal, but it cannot substitute for institutional controls. If preventing abuse depends on individual agents risking dismissal after political appointees have already mobilized federal power, the system is relying on conscience at the final stage of a process designed above their heads.

The seizure can become the sabotage

The danger described by officials is concrete even without proving that a future operation has already been planned. Removing ballots or machines can obstruct voting or counting and disturb the chain of custody used to establish that election materials were not altered.

That disruption can then manufacture the uncertainty invoked to justify it. Federal authorities act on unsupported fraud claims; their intervention compromises ordinary election procedures; the resulting disorder becomes material for further suspicion. The government does not need to prove fraud to damage confidence. It can create a procedural mess and point to the mess.

The framing understates responsibility

Calling this a fear that agents might become “tools” risks making the bureau sound like an inert object caught in somebody else’s scheme. Institutions act through people. A U.S. attorney who advances baseless allegations, an FBI official who approves a dubious operation, or an agent who knowingly executes an improper seizure each exercises agency at a different level of power.

The reporting itself supplies the sharper frame: officials fear that at least some federal personnel would cooperate. Conservative agents and progressive legal groups may now share an interest in preventing election interference, but that unusual alignment is not the main political fact. The main fact is that internal compliance can convert partisan election denial into state action.

The systemic error

Election subversion does not require every official to embrace it. It requires political leaders willing to apply pressure, enough institutional gatekeepers willing to comply, and a bureaucracy that makes refusal personally costly.

That is the larger pattern exposed here. False claims can acquire coercive force when prosecutors, warrants, armed agents, and disciplinary authority are placed behind them. The system fails long before ballots are physically removed: it fails when obedience is rewarded, resistance is punished, and officials treat the deliberate use of public power against election administration as merely an ethical dilemma for individual employees.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump's plan to make America safe for gangsters
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that The Bulwark columnist Jonathan V. Last accused President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio of helping Flávio Bolsonaro enter the United States and obtain a visa while Bolsonaro faced charges in Brazil. According to Last, Rubio arranged the assistance with Trump’s approval and acted clandestinely to bend or disregard US law. The article supplies no government response, documentary evidence, details of the charges, or independent confirmation of th
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that The Bulwark columnist Jonathan V. Last accused President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio of helping Flávio Bolsonaro enter the United States and obtain a visa while Bolsonaro faced charges in Brazil. According to Last, Rubio arranged the assistance with Trump’s approval and acted clandestinely to bend or disregard US law. The article supplies no government response, documentary evidence, details of the charges, or independent confirmation of that account.

Last argues that the episode exposes selective enforcement behind the administration’s anti-immigration rhetoric: suspected criminality becomes disqualifying for politically useful targets but negotiable for an ally from the Bolsonaro family. He presents the alleged intervention as protection for a political associate facing accountability abroad.

The power sits in Washington

The decisive actors in this account are not migrants, prosecutors, or border agents. They are the president and secretary of state, officials with authority over diplomacy and substantial influence over visa policy. If Last’s description is accurate, Rubio enabled the entry and Trump sanctioned it.

That distinction matters because immigration enforcement is routinely sold as an impersonal defense of law. Here, the allegation is that senior officials treated the law as adjustable from above. The weak are processed by the system; the connected may receive a customized system.

Criminality as a political category

The administration’s rhetoric, as described by Last, links immigration with gangs and violent disorder. But the alleged assistance to Bolsonaro suggests that “criminal” is not functioning as a consistent legal category. It is functioning as a label applied to disfavored people and suspended for favored ones.

The article’s strongest political point is therefore not that one visa contradicts one slogan. It is that punitive language can conceal discretionary power. Officials invoke danger to justify harsh treatment of broad populations, then reserve exceptions for ideological allies. That is hierarchy dressed as enforcement.

What the framing fails to prove

AlterNet largely relays Last’s conclusions instead of establishing the underlying case. It calls the assistance asylum in one passage and discusses a visa in another, without explaining the legal mechanism or distinction. It also does not identify which laws Rubio allegedly bent or ignored, when Bolsonaro entered, what charges he faced, or whether US authorities considered those charges in granting the visa.

Those omissions do not vindicate the administration. They limit what can responsibly be claimed. Last alleges official favoritism and legal manipulation; the supplied reporting does not independently demonstrate them. A serious account of abuse of power requires more than a columnist’s certainty, especially when the central accusation concerns clandestine conduct.

The useful misdirection

The public argument is steered toward whether particular migrants are dangerous. That keeps attention on people with little institutional power while obscuring who decides which rules are enforced, against whom, and with what exceptions.

If the reported intervention occurred as Last describes, the relevant danger is not inconsistency in political messaging. It is executive discretion used to sort human beings by political usefulness. The consequence is a two-tier regime: maximum suspicion for designated outsiders, privileged access for allies of the governing faction.

Impunity recognizes its own

Last interprets Trump’s affinity for the Bolsonaro family as solidarity among political figures hostile to legal restraint. The article does not prove that motive, but the alleged conduct fits a broader and more concrete pattern: leaders who campaign on uncompromising order often preserve their widest mercy for the powerful and connected.

That is the systemic lesson. “Law and order” can mean aggressive control below and personalized exemption above. The slogan directs fear toward weaker actors; the machinery of government determines who actually receives protection.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: No victory for bus driver fired over 'Jesus' candy
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened A federal judge dismissed with prejudice former Mattawan Consolidated School District bus driver Sarah Robinson’s lawsuit over her April 2025 firing, meaning she cannot refile the case. According to AlterNet, the Michigan district fired Robinson after she repeatedly distributed Christian messages and candy to children on her route despite instructions to stop. Robinson first handed out the bags in 2024. After a Jewish parent complained, the district prohibited further distribution
item.content:encoded:
What happened

A federal judge dismissed with prejudice former Mattawan Consolidated School District bus driver Sarah Robinson’s lawsuit over her April 2025 firing, meaning she cannot refile the case. According to AlterNet, the Michigan district fired Robinson after she repeatedly distributed Christian messages and candy to children on her route despite instructions to stop.

Robinson first handed out the bags in 2024. After a Jewish parent complained, the district prohibited further distribution of religious materials. Before Easter, Robinson had her daughter and her daughter’s friend distribute candy instead. U.S. District Judge Jane M. Beckering ruled that Robinson remained a district employee with duties toward the children even while the bus was stationary and that the students constituted a captive audience.

AlterNet, citing Friendly Atheist, reports that Robinson represented herself while using an attorney only to draft her complaint. Beckering also identified basic defects in her case, including missing exhibits and a failure to name anyone who allegedly violated her constitutional rights.

The district held the power—and used it properly

The school district controlled Robinson’s employment and set the conditions under which its employees interacted with students. It exercised that authority after receiving a parent’s complaint, instructing Robinson not to distribute religious materials on the bus.

That order did not suppress Robinson’s private faith. It restricted what a public employee could press upon children entrusted to her care. The distinction is elementary: Robinson could practice Christianity; she could not use a government job and a school-controlled setting to evangelize a religiously diverse group of minors.

This was defiance, not confusion

The decisive act was not the first bag. Robinson might plausibly have misunderstood an initial supervisor’s permission to distribute optional candy. That explanation collapsed once the district explicitly told her to stop distributing religious material.

Her later use of her daughter and another child to hand out candy was an attempted workaround. The district could reasonably treat that maneuver as evidence that another warning would not secure compliance. Robinson had already shown that she understood the restriction well enough to route around it.

A captive audience is not a congregation

Robinson compared herself to football coach Joe Kennedy, whose postgame midfield prayer produced a Supreme Court victory. Beckering rejected the analogy because Robinson was still performing her job and still responsible for students’ safe boarding and departure.

More importantly, children riding an assigned school bus are not ordinary passersby encountering private religious expression. They depend on the driver and the district for transportation. Calling participation “optional” does not erase that power imbalance or convert a public-school route into Robinson’s personal mission field.

The persecution story reverses responsibility

The grievance narrative casts Robinson as a Christian punished for speaking about Jesus. The reported sequence shows something narrower and less flattering: an employee received a direct workplace instruction, disregarded it, and then claimed constitutional injury when the employer imposed consequences.

That framing also pushes the burden onto the Jewish parent whose complaint forced the district to confront the practice. The parent did not wield institutional power over Robinson. The district did. Treating the complaint as the source of the conflict obscures Robinson’s decision to use public employment for sectarian messaging—and her subsequent decision to continue after being told to stop.

Privilege becomes principle when challenged

The larger pattern is the conversion of access into entitlement. A public employee assumes a government-controlled audience is available for personal religious advocacy; resistance is then recast as discrimination, and ordinary accountability becomes alleged persecution.

Beckering’s ruling, as reported, refused that inversion. Religious liberty protects belief and private expression. It does not grant public employees a superior claim over children in their custody, nor does it require institutions to indulge deliberate noncompliance merely because the employee describes it as faith.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy fell eight percentage points behind Democrat Amy Acton in a private poll commissioned by a Republican group. Acton had led by two points less than 10 days earlier, before Ramaswamy’s attack ad began airing on October 19. The article does not provide the poll’s methodology, field dates, or year, so its findings establish Republican concern—not a settled electoral outcome.

The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar. The public then learned, according to the reporting, that the mother had left decades earlier with Acton’s sexually abusive stepfather. Republicans had warned Ramaswamy against the attack, but President Donald Trump endorsed it as “hitting pay dirt,” while Vice President JD Vance told critics to “stop whining.”

The reported backlash has Republicans worried about damage beyond the governor’s race, particularly to Senator Jon Husted’s reelection bid and potentially Senate control. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine called the ad wrong and urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it; Trump attacked DeWine in response. Campaign figures are now blaming Ramaswamy for insisting that the ad run.

The power was never mysterious

Ramaswamy reportedly pushed for the ad. His campaign aired it. Trump and Vance used their authority inside the Republican Party to defend it after its cruelty became apparent. Those are decisions made by powerful political actors, not an unfortunate communications mishap produced by nobody in particular.

DeWine objected, but his objection also clarifies the hierarchy. A sitting Republican governor could call the attack wrong; Trump could answer by accusing him of wanting a Democrat to win. The message was blunt: loyalty to the party’s dominant figure outranks judgment, restraint, and even protection of the broader ticket.

Polling changed the moral calculus

The Republican alarm described here is not principally about what the ad did to Acton. It is about what the ad might do to Republicans.

Before the poll, some party figures warned that exploiting a painful family history crossed a line. After the poll showed an eight-point deficit, insiders began emphasizing who demanded the ad and who opposed it. The conduct remained the same. What changed was its apparent electoral price.

That is damage control masquerading as accountability. “Vivek got what he wanted” shifts responsibility onto one candidate while leaving intact the political culture that rewards personal degradation when strategists believe it works.

The backlash did not create the offense

Coverage built around GOP “knives” and internal panic risks making Republican infighting the central event. It is not. The central event is that a campaign weaponized an estranged relative and a history involving alleged sexual abuse, then received public encouragement from the president and vice president.

Calling the result “backlash” can also obscure agency. Voters did not mysteriously become upset; the campaign supplied a reason. Nor did the ad merely “cross a line,” as if political boundaries enforce themselves. Named officials chose to air it, defend it, or oppose it.

The private poll may suggest a reaction, but without methodological details it cannot prove that the ad alone caused the six-point movement in Acton’s reported margin. The attached memo’s conclusion that the ad was having a significant effect remains the assessment of the Republican group behind the survey.

Cruelty as a party test

Trump’s response to DeWine turned a dispute over campaign conduct into a loyalty test. Rather than address whether the ad was defensible, he questioned DeWine’s partisan allegiance and praised the attack’s tactical value. Vance likewise treated criticism as weakness.

That pattern matters more than the consultants’ finger-pointing. When leaders define any usable wound as legitimate ammunition, cruelty becomes evidence of commitment. Objections are recast as sabotage; restraint becomes assistance to the enemy.

The predictable consequence is institutional cowardice. Party operatives may recognize the harm, but many speak clearly only when polling suggests that the harm could cost them power.

The system rewards remorse on a delay

This episode reveals a political apparatus with abundant agency and highly selective responsibility. Candidates authorize attacks. Party leaders validate them. Operatives distribute them. Then, if voters recoil, the same structure describes itself as “reeling,” as though it were struck by an external force.

The deeper failure is not that one attack ad may have backfired. It is that the party’s internal mechanism for rejecting the attack appears weaker than its mechanism for measuring the electoral damage afterward. In that system, conscience arrives only after the polling memo.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The Talent Shortage Starts at the Filter
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
How employers exclude capable people, then complain they cannot find them.

Apparently, the ideal employee has considerable experience, modest salary expectations, no employment gaps, no inconvenient commitments, and absolutely no history of changing jobs.

They should bring fresh thinking while having done this exact job before. They should be ambitious enough to impress, but never so ambitious that they might leave.

And if they are looking for work, they should avoid appearing too available.

A LinkedIn graphic listing familiar hiring prejudices captures this absurdity: experienced candidates dismissed as overqualified, career breaks treated as suspicious, and entry-level vacancies demanding years of experience.

Each assumption can sound reasonable in isolation. Together, they describe a system in which almost any human life contains grounds for rejection.

Then comes the complaint: we cannot find the right people.

Before accepting that diagnosis, we should examine the machinery producing it.

When a shortcut becomes a verdict

Hiring involves uncertainty. A CV cannot tell an employer everything about someone’s judgment, reliability, or ability to learn. Interviews offer incomplete evidence. Mistakes can be expensive.

So employers use shortcuts.

A degree suggests knowledge. Continuous employment suggests stability. A familiar job title suggests relevant experience. These signals can provide useful information.

The trouble begins when a signal becomes a substitute for investigation.

An employment gap establishes that someone spent time outside recorded employment. It does not establish that they lost their competence. Several short jobs establish a pattern worth discussing. They do not explain whether the cause was poor performance, temporary contracts, repeated restructuring, or employers making promises they did not keep.

“Overqualified” is similarly unfinished reasoning. Perhaps the candidate will dislike the work or expect more money than the budget allows. Those are questions an employer can ask. Rejecting someone before asking turns an imagined answer into a hiring decision.

The applicant supplies a fact. The employer supplies a story. The story becomes the verdict.

The people the process makes invisible

This problem extends beyond anecdotes.

The 2021 Harvard Business School and Accenture report Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent documented how recruitment systems can exclude potentially qualified applicants through restrictive screening criteria. Among employers surveyed, 48% filtered candidates for middle-skills roles based on employment gaps exceeding six months. A rule about chronology could therefore prevent someone’s abilities from reaching a recruiter at all. Read the report.

That distinction matters. A person rejected after a relevant assessment has at least been evaluated against the work. Someone removed by a crude filter may never receive that assessment.

Their absence from the shortlist can subsequently be mistaken for evidence that suitable candidates do not exist.

The process has helped create the shortage it reports.

That does not explain every unfilled vacancy. Some occupations face real constraints in training, location, or available expertise. But a company cannot credibly diagnose its own talent shortage without examining whom its rules exclude.

Whose risk counts?

Consider what the recruitment process asks each side to tolerate.

An employer may expect applicants to complete assessments, attend several interviews, and explain every career transition before revealing what the job pays.

The candidate must demonstrate commitment while lacking information essential to deciding whether the opportunity is viable.

That arrangement shifts the cost of uncertainty onto the person with less power.

The same imbalance appears in demands for immediate productivity. Requiring someone to have already performed an almost identical role can reduce the employer’s training burden. It also narrows the route into the profession.

An entry-level position requiring substantial prior experience leaves an obvious question: who is supposed to provide the entry?

Training takes money and management attention. Employers have legitimate reasons to weigh those costs. But when they choose to avoid them, they should acknowledge the tradeoff. A hiring policy that excludes people who need development will produce a smaller pool.

That outcome should hardly be surprising.

Changing the advertisement is easier than changing the decision

Corporate reform often begins with better language.

A company announces that it values skills over credentials. Degree requirements disappear from its advertisements. The announcement becomes evidence of progress.

The actual hiring decisions deserve closer attention.

A 2024 study by Harvard Business School and the Burning Glass Institute found that approximately 45% of the firms studied that removed degree requirements showed no meaningful change in hiring behavior afterward. Nearly all the observed change came from 37% of the firms. Read the research summary.

The implication is uncomfortable: an organization can remove a formal barrier while continuing to favor the same backgrounds through interviews, informal preferences, and managerial expectations.

Without a credible way to assess ability, familiar credentials can quietly resume their old role.

AI inherits the question we ask it

Automated recruitment promises relief from crowded inboxes and inconsistent decisions. There are useful tasks software can perform in a hiring process.

But giving a machine responsibility for a shortlist does not resolve the question of what qualifies someone to be on it.

If a system uses uninterrupted employment as evidence of competence, people with career breaks face the consequences of that assumption. If it rewards resemblance to previous hires, existing patterns can become instructions for future selection.

Whether a particular tool does this requires evidence about that tool. The underlying design problem is straightforward: automation can execute a poor hiring rule efficiently.

An employer remains responsible for deciding what the system measures, checking its results, and providing a way to challenge mistakes.

A score cannot carry that responsibility.

Make the standard answerable

Better hiring requires standards that employers can explain in relation to the work.

What must this person accomplish? Which abilities are essential on arrival? Which can be taught? What evidence would demonstrate each one?

Those questions lead to practical changes: publish the pay range early, use consistent questions, assess relevant work through proportionate exercises, and investigate career histories without presuming guilt.

They also require scrutiny of comforting phrases.

If “culture fit” means respectful collaboration, define the behavior and assess it consistently. If it means a manager felt immediately comfortable with someone, the organization should recognize how little that feeling establishes about performance.

For every rejection criterion, there should be an answer to a simple question:

What evidence connects this requirement to doing the job well?

Some requirements will survive that scrutiny. Others will turn out to be habits with official-looking names.

Employers cannot eliminate uncertainty from hiring. They can decide whether to investigate it or disguise it as certainty about someone they have barely assessed.

And before declaring that the talent is missing, they should check the people their process has been instructed to overlook.

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Texas Already Let Its Power Grid Kill 246 People. Now Greg Abbott Is Worried About AI.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The 2021 freeze exposed the consequences of inadequate regulation. Five years later, Texas is discovering that data centers don’t negotiate with physics. item.content:encoded:
The 2021 freeze exposed the consequences of inadequate regulation. Five years later, Texas is discovering that data centers don’t negotiate with physics.

In February 2021, Texas experienced one of the most catastrophic failures of electrical infrastructure in modern American history.

Millions of people lost power.

Homes became dangerously cold. Water systems failed. Families struggled to find heat, clean drinking water, and shelter.

According to the Texas Department of State Health Services, 246 people died as a result of the disaster.

Five years later, Governor Greg Abbott is sounding the alarm about another threat to the state’s electricity grid.

Artificial intelligence.

Apparently, when the potential victims are ordinary Texans freezing in their homes, the argument for minimal government intervention can survive astonishingly well.

When multibillion-dollar data centers threaten to overwhelm the electricity system, suddenly regulation becomes indispensable.

The underlying problem, however, is much older than AI.

The Disaster Texas Was Warned About

The February 2021 catastrophe is commonly associated with Winter Storm Uri.

An extraordinary cold front swept across Texas, overwhelming electricity generation and natural-gas infrastructure.

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas — ERCOT — was forced to disconnect approximately 20,000 megawatts of electricity demand to prevent an even more devastating grid collapse.

More than 4.5 million people lost electricity, some for days.

But the most damning aspect of the disaster wasn’t the weather.

It was the warning.

In February 2011, Texas had experienced another serious winter electricity emergency.

Federal investigators examined the event and recommended improvements to cold-weather preparedness.

A decade later, many of those lessons had still not been adequately implemented.

In September 2021, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Chairman Rich Glick acknowledged that recommendations following the earlier disaster had not been acted upon.

That is a remarkable admission.

Texas didn’t simply encounter an unforeseeable natural disaster.

Its institutions had been warned about a class of failure, and the necessary preparations remained insufficient.

The result was measured in human lives.

Deregulation Doesn’t Repeal Thermodynamics

Texas has long presented its electricity system as a model of competitive energy markets.

The state’s wholesale electricity market was designed to rely heavily on price signals and competition rather than the more centralized planning arrangements used elsewhere.

Supporters argued that competition would improve efficiency and restrain costs.

Critics warned that a market emphasizing short-term economic incentives could underprovide reliability investments whose benefits become apparent only during emergencies.

Winterization costs money.

Maintaining reserve capacity costs money.

Protecting natural-gas infrastructure from extreme cold costs money.

And the financial incentives to make those investments aren’t necessarily aligned with their social value.

If the market doesn’t adequately reward reliability, companies can have strong incentives to minimize expenditures that protect the public against rare but devastating events.

The consequences become everybody else’s problem.

Now, we should be precise: deregulation was not the sole cause of the February 2021 catastrophe. Extreme weather, failed generating equipment, natural-gas supply disruptions, inadequate winterization, and limited connections to neighboring grids all contributed.

But the regulatory framework determines which precautions are required, which risks are tolerated, and who bears the consequences when those risks become reality.

That makes regulatory policy central to the story.

And Texas’s political leadership cannot simply point at the weather and declare the matter closed.

Enter the Data Centers

Fast-forward to 2026.

The artificial intelligence boom has triggered an extraordinary race to construct computing infrastructure.

Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, particularly facilities packed with high-performance AI accelerators.

And Texas, with its large energy industry, available land, and established technology infrastructure, became an attractive destination.

There was just one complication.

All those data centers needed electricity.

Lots of it.

By August 2026, ERCOT was facing more than 1,800 large-load interconnection proposals, representing over 474 gigawatts of potential demand. Roughly 90% of those projects were data centers.

For comparison, that proposed total was more than five times the historical peak demand of the entire Texas grid.

Now, there’s an important qualification.

Those 474 gigawatts aren’t actual consumption.

They’re proposed connections, many of which may never become operational. Some projects lack financing, committed customers, or sufficiently developed construction plans.

Counting every application as guaranteed future demand would be misleading.

But even allowing for speculative applications, the volume reveals a serious planning problem.

ERCOT’s old process, which evaluated major connection requests individually, was no longer adequate for the scale of proposed development.

In June 2026, regulators approved a new framework called Batch Zero, allowing qualified large projects to be studied together so the operator could assess their combined effects on the system.

In other words, grid development required coordinated planning.

Not simply another round of companies competing to be first in line.

Suddenly, Regulation Is a Wonderful Idea

On August 3, 2026, Greg Abbott ordered an audit of proposed data centers seeking access to the Texas grid, interrupting the normal approval process.

On September 21, he went further, ordering a halt to new state permits for data-center projects until electricity and water-resource reviews were completed.

The governor declared that Texans must come first.

He insisted that data centers should pay for the infrastructure they require, protect electricity reliability, account for their water consumption, and avoid imposing additional burdens on residential customers.

Taken on their own terms, these are reasonable public-policy objectives.

Large private consumers should not be allowed to transfer their infrastructure costs and environmental burdens onto the public without scrutiny.

But that raises an uncomfortable question.

Why did Texas need a catastrophe in 2021 to demonstrate the importance of adequate electricity regulation, and another looming infrastructure crisis in 2026 to make coordinated oversight politically urgent?

This isn’t an argument against the new restrictions.

It’s an argument for remembering why those restrictions are necessary in the first place.

Government oversight isn’t merely something to introduce when private industry’s requirements become inconvenient.

Its purpose is to anticipate risks, establish enforceable requirements, and protect the public before foreseeable failures become disasters.

The Myth of a Self-Regulating Grid

The deeper contradiction is philosophical.

Modern electricity infrastructure is an interconnected engineering system.

Power plants, transmission networks, substations, fuel suppliers, maintenance crews, consumers, and system operators must function together.

The system must balance electricity supply and demand continuously.

And it must remain reliable under conditions that cannot be predicted with perfect precision.

None of this can be managed through price signals alone.

Markets are powerful tools for allocating resources.

They are not substitutes for engineering standards, mandatory safety requirements, infrastructure planning, or emergency preparedness.

A power plant operator may determine that an expensive winterization upgrade is unlikely to provide an adequate private financial return.

The families depending on that plant during a catastrophic freeze have an entirely different calculation.

A data-center developer may reasonably conclude that building in Texas maximizes expected returns.

Residents whose electricity bills rise to finance network upgrades, or whose communities face greater water stress, may reach another conclusion.

That’s precisely why public regulation exists.

The problem isn’t that businesses pursue their economic interests.

The problem arises when institutions allow private financial decisions to impose risks and costs on people who never consented to them.

And Now the AI Industry Wants Its Share

There’s an additional irony.

Artificial intelligence companies are not requesting a modest extension of ordinary electricity consumption.

They are proposing infrastructure projects on a scale that can reshape regional energy planning.

Some facilities may need dedicated transmission upgrades, new substations, additional generating capacity, or substantial water resources.

Those requirements create legitimate questions about cost allocation.

Who pays for a transmission upgrade built primarily to serve a private data center?

What happens if the company abandons the project after the infrastructure is constructed?

Should residential customers subsidize electrical capacity reserved for speculative developments?

Who compensates communities for local resource burdens?

And how much risk should a public electricity system assume in response to forecasts generated by companies competing for market share?

These are not anti-technology questions.

They’re basic governance questions.

The AI industry has every right to develop commercially useful infrastructure within applicable law.

It does not have an inherent right to privatize the profits while socializing the costs.

Nor does the promise of future technological progress excuse governments from protecting the people who live alongside that infrastructure.

The Convenient Discovery of Government

Following the 2021 disaster, Texas enacted new reliability and weatherization requirements.

Those reforms matter, and dismissing them entirely would obscure the historical record.

But reforms introduced after a catastrophe don’t erase the earlier failure to act on known risks.

Nor does the introduction of stricter data-center oversight in 2026 resolve the broader political contradiction.

For decades, deregulation was sold as a way to unleash the efficiency of private enterprise.

The 2021 freeze demonstrated the human consequences when infrastructure resilience is inadequate.

The AI expansion is now demonstrating how private investment decisions can create demands far beyond what existing public systems were designed to accommodate.

And suddenly, the same state government finds itself insisting on audits, infrastructure obligations, mandatory reporting, and regulatory approvals.

All essential functions of government.

All functions that become considerably harder to perform after a crisis has already begun.

The Price of Learning the Same Lesson Twice

There is nothing inherently wrong with building more data centers.

There is nothing inherently wrong with developing artificial intelligence.

And there is certainly nothing wrong with expanding electricity generation and transmission capacity to meet genuinely useful economic demand.

The question is how those investments are planned, regulated, and paid for.

Texas has already demonstrated what happens when critical infrastructure is insufficiently prepared for foreseeable extremes.

In 2021, the consequence was a humanitarian disaster.

In 2026, the immediate challenge is the extraordinary scale of proposed industrial electricity consumption.

The situations are different.

The underlying lesson is not.

Essential infrastructure cannot be governed as though public safety were merely another variable in a private company’s quarterly earnings calculation.

Abbott’s new restrictions acknowledge that reality, at least in the context of data centers.

What remains is the uncomfortable history behind that acknowledgement.

A decade of warnings preceded the 2021 freeze.

Two hundred and forty-six officially documented deaths followed.

Now Texas is once again confronting the consequences of an electricity system facing demands its existing arrangements cannot simply absorb.

Perhaps the state will manage this expansion more successfully.

But the central lesson shouldn’t require another emergency to become politically acceptable.

Physics does not care about deregulation slogans.

And electricity grids do not become more reliable simply because their failures are inconvenient to the politicians responsible for overseeing them.

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The AI Bubble May Burst. The Revolution Won’t.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Wall Street can get the economics of artificial intelligence spectacularly wrong without making the technology itself any less real. There is a peculiar obsession spreading across the Internet: the imminent collapse of artificial intelligence. Every few days, another video, financial analyst, or technology commentator announces that the AI bubble is about to burst. Billions are being spent on data centers. Electricity grids are struggling. Specialized chips become outdated. Investors are lending
item.content:encoded:
Wall Street can get the economics of artificial intelligence spectacularly wrong without making the technology itself any less real.

There is a peculiar obsession spreading across the Internet: the imminent collapse of artificial intelligence.

Every few days, another video, financial analyst, or technology commentator announces that the AI bubble is about to burst. Billions are being spent on data centers. Electricity grids are struggling. Specialized chips become outdated. Investors are lending enormous amounts of money to companies that have yet to demonstrate sustainable profitability.

Therefore, we are told, the entire AI revolution is approaching its inevitable reckoning.

There is just one problem with this argument.

It confuses the price of a revolution with the reality of the revolution itself.

And history has an extraordinary amount to say about that mistake.

The Bubble Is Not the Technology

Let’s establish something immediately: there are legitimate reasons to be concerned about the economics of artificial intelligence.

According to J.P. Morgan’s October 2026 research, global AI capital expenditure could approach $900 billion this year alone, with cumulative investment projected at $5.5 trillion by 2030.

Those are astonishing amounts of money.

Companies are constructing enormous data centers, purchasing GPUs by the thousands, arranging long-term electricity contracts, and financing infrastructure whose economic returns remain uncertain.

Some investments will turn out to be brilliant.

Others will be catastrophic.

And some companies currently valued at extraordinary multiples may eventually discover that investors are no longer willing to subsidize their ambitions.

None of that means artificial intelligence doesn’t work.

It means Wall Street may be overpaying for something that works.

Those are radically different propositions.

Consider the Internet.

We’ve Seen This Movie Before

In the late 1990s, investors became convinced that the Internet would transform virtually every industry.

They were right.

They also became convinced that almost any company with a website deserved an astronomical valuation.

They were spectacularly wrong.

The dot-com bubble burst. Companies disappeared. Investors lost fortunes. The Nasdaq collapsed.

And then something rather inconvenient happened to the people who treated the crash as proof that the Internet had been overhyped.

The Internet kept growing.

Amazon survived. Google expanded. Online commerce flourished. Streaming emerged. Cloud computing transformed enterprise infrastructure. Smartphones made the Internet effectively ubiquitous.

The technological revolution didn’t fail.

The financial speculation surrounding it did.

The same pattern had occurred during Britain’s nineteenth-century railway mania.

Investors poured extraordinary sums into railway companies, many of which were financially unsustainable. The resulting crash destroyed wealth and ruined families.

But the railways didn’t vanish.

They became the circulatory system of industrial economies.

And then came telecommunications.

During the late-1990s fiber-optic boom, companies buried immense quantities of cable across continents and beneath oceans. Much of it initially went unused.

Financially, the overbuilding was disastrous.

Technologically, it created infrastructure that later supported an explosion of Internet traffic.

The investors who paid for the future didn’t necessarily profit from it. But the future arrived anyway.

Physics Doesn’t Care About Your Market Capitalization

The latest warnings about AI infrastructure do contain something genuinely important.

Power grids cannot expand at the speed of software development.

A company can purchase another thousand GPUs with a procurement order. It cannot manufacture a transmission network, build substations, produce enormous transformers, and train thousands of electricians overnight.

Texas, for example, has been overwhelmed by proposed large electricity loads, most associated with data centers. Virginia faces its own substantial interconnection delays.

But there’s an important distinction here, too.

A request to connect a data center to an electrical grid is not proof that the center will actually be constructed.

Developers routinely explore multiple sites. Projects are postponed, redesigned, or canceled. Adding every proposed megawatt together and presenting the result as inevitable consumption is misleading.

The bottleneck is real.

The conclusion that it spells the end of AI is not.

And there’s another detail worth considering.

Infrastructure constraints create incentives for engineering solutions.

More efficient processors. Better cooling systems. Improved model architectures. Quantization. Distillation. Smarter workload scheduling. More efficient inference.

Every one of those technologies can reduce the computing power needed to deliver a given result.

The industry doesn’t need to solve every infrastructure problem by building another gigantic data center.

Sometimes the solution is to make the existing hardware do more.

In computing, we’ve spent decades doing exactly that.

The Economics of Artificial Intelligence Are Not the Same as Its Utility

Here’s another mistake that keeps appearing in these discussions.

People look at the money AI companies spend, compare it with their revenue, and conclude that the technology must be commercially unsustainable.

But that calculation misses an essential distinction.

The value created by a technology is not necessarily captured entirely by the company selling it.

Consider a programmer using AI to complete in two hours a task that previously required two days.

The AI provider might earn twenty dollars per month from that customer.

The programmer might save thousands of dollars’ worth of labor over the same period.

The value exists.

It simply doesn’t all appear on the AI provider’s income statement.

And this is not hypothetical.

For years, developers have been using AI to generate code, explain unfamiliar systems, write tests, investigate failures, and accelerate debugging.

I’ve personally used AI in production software development for more than three years.

It isn’t magic. It isn’t infallible. And blindly accepting generated code is a spectacularly bad engineering practice.

But properly integrated into a development workflow, it is an extremely powerful productivity tool.

The question isn’t whether that productivity exists.

The question is how much customers will ultimately pay for it, which companies will capture that revenue, and whether their margins can justify their infrastructure investments.

That’s a business question.

Not a referendum on the validity of the technology.

The Hardware Obsolescence Argument Has a Hole in It

One of the more dramatic claims in the bubble narrative is that AI companies are filling warehouses with expensive chips that will become obsolete before they can be powered on.

There is a genuine concern about hardware depreciation.

But newer hardware doesn’t magically render older hardware useless.

A new GPU may deliver substantially more computing power per watt. It may support larger models or higher-throughput inference.

That doesn’t mean the previous generation suddenly stops being able to perform useful calculations.

Not every AI workload requires the newest accelerator.

Smaller models, specialized applications, batch processing, inference, research, and many enterprise tasks can continue running on older hardware.

Eventually, economics determines which jobs make sense on which machines.

A graphics card that is no longer competitive for training the world’s largest frontier model may still be extremely useful for thousands of less demanding workloads.

The relevant question is not whether newer hardware exists.

It’s whether older hardware can continue generating enough value to justify its operating costs.

And that answer isn’t automatically zero.

Follow the Money — But Follow the Value Too

There are legitimate financial concerns surrounding the AI industry.

Some companies are investing in their own customers. Some data-center projects rely on complicated financing arrangements. Some hardware manufacturers have extended depreciation schedules, improving reported earnings.

Investors absolutely should scrutinize those arrangements.

And if companies knowingly misrepresent asset values, conceal material liabilities, or fabricate revenue, regulators should investigate and enforce the law.

But unusual financing isn’t automatically fraud.

Neither is an accounting estimate that turns out to be optimistic.

The stronger criticism is that financial incentives can encourage companies to overinvest, exaggerate future demand, and distribute the consequences of failure to creditors, pension funds, employees, and smaller investors.

That deserves serious attention.

What it doesn’t justify is pretending the technology underneath the financial structure is worthless.

What Happens After the Bubble Bursts?

Suppose the pessimists are correct.

Suppose investment collapses. Valuations fall. AI startups go bankrupt. Hyperscalers cancel projects. Investors write down billions in assets.

What happens next?

The models don’t disappear.

The research doesn’t vanish.

The engineers don’t forget what they’ve learned.

The functioning data centers don’t spontaneously stop operating.

The software already integrated into businesses doesn’t magically revert to its pre-AI state.

Some companies acquire distressed assets at a discount. Others consolidate. More efficient competitors replace less efficient ones.

And customers continue demanding useful services.

There may even be a significant benefit: infrastructure purchased at inflated prices during the boom could eventually become available at much lower costs.

The tragedy would be borne by investors, workers, communities, and anyone whose savings or livelihood became tied to unsustainable financial commitments.

The technology itself would continue evolving.

Just as the Internet did.

Just as telecommunications did.

Just as railways did.

The Wrong Question

Every technological revolution attracts speculation.

Investors see an enormous potential market. They compete to capture it. Optimistic forecasts become extravagant valuations. Money flows faster than reality can justify.

Sometimes the resulting bubble bursts.

But a financial bubble is not a technological verdict.

The real questions aren’t whether AI spending is sustainable at today’s levels, whether every data center will be profitable, or whether every company promising artificial intelligence will survive.

Some won’t.

The more important question is whether the underlying technology creates lasting economic and practical value.

And on that point, we already have substantial evidence that it does.

The AI bubble may burst.

The AI revolution doesn’t need the bubble to survive.

History has demonstrated the difference repeatedly.

Perhaps it’s time we learned it.

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: AI Didn’t Kill Evidence. It Killed “Trust Me, It’s Real.”
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A 15-year-old girl in Florida apparently wanted to frame her ex-boyfriend. Not long ago, accomplishing that convincingly might have required considerable technical ability.
